title: Spain’s Mediapro Group To Become Imagina After Reorganization
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Royal Period Drama ‘Queen Silvia’ To Get World Premiere Screening At MIPCOM Cannes Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull Kayleigh Llewellyn Adapting Sarah Waters Novel ‘The Paying Guests’ For BBC Studios Fiction View All September 10, 2026 6:26am Mediapro Executive Chairman Sergio Oslé and CEO Carlos Núñez Grup Mediapro Spain ‘s Grup Mediapro will relaunch as Imagina on January 1, 2027, following a major company review. The decision to relaunch comes after “several months of reorganization” and was announced internally yesterday at an all-staff meeting. “The change revives a name the group has used before across its more than 30-year history, reflecting its intent to look ahead while staying grounded in its past,” the company said in a note to press. Imagina was previously the parent company of Mediapro, following the latter’s 2006 merger with producer Globomedia. Related Stories News Woody Allen To Start Shooting Next Project In Spain In October Executives HBO Max Names Movistar Plus+ Film Chief & 'Sirat' Producer Guillermo Farré As Original Production Chief In Spain The news follows a tumultuous 2026 for the Spanish sports media and entertainment giant, during which it cut 189 staff. Senior execs such as General Manager Laura Fernández Espeso, The Mediapro Studio’s international content chief, Ran Tellem, and business chief Miguel Cardenal all left. Watch on Deadline Mediapro’s new management, Executive Chairman Sergio Oslé and CEO Carlos Núñez, said the company expects EBITDA to grow between 50% and 60% against 2025, along with positive cash flow generation. This was thanks to the company-wide review that took place over the first months of 2026 and ultimately “brought its resources in line with today’s market realities.” “The next step is to drive new projects that deliver unique experiences to audiences around the world, funding this growth with more than €100 million [$116 million] the company itself will generate over the next three years,” the company stated. Oslé and Nũnez were installed following the departures of founding partners Jaume Roures and Tatxo Benet. They are now presiding over a business that handles production of numerous major sporting events, sells broadcast rights to the likes of Spain’s La Liga outside of North America, MENA and India, and has a content production unit that is behind the likes of The Head . Southwind Media Capital, which is part of China’s Orient Hontai Capital, owns Mediapro, which has its main offices in Madrid and Barcelona. Southwind bought a majority stake in February 2018, with former bosses Roures and Benet retaining minority stakes. title: ‘Le Faux Soir’ Trailer: Arieh Worthalter & Mélanie Thierry Star In WW2 Belgian Resistance “Media Hack” Drama – TIFF
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘No Other Land’ Co-Directors Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor Lift Lid On New Bombshell Doc ‘Naza’ Exposing Israel’s Deliberate Targeting Of Civilian Homes In Gaza – Venice Ellen Burstyn Talks Working Into 90s with Starring Role In Unexpected Love Story ‘Place To Be’; Pays Tribute To Gloria Steinem – Venice First Behind-The Scenes Look Reveals Isabelle Huppert As Crime Boss In Yann Demange’s London-Set ‘Lineage’ View All September 10, 2026 6:26am EXCLUSIVE: Michaël R. Roskam‘s ensemble World War Two Belgian resistance drama Le Faux Soir world premieres as a Special Presentation in Toronto this weekend, before heading to San Sebastian as the closing film, and Deadline can unveil the trailer. Set in Belgium in November 1943, the drama is inspired by the events surrounding daily newspaper Le Soir, which became a vehicle for Nazi Germany propaganda following its invasion of the country in 1940, resulting in it being nicknamed “Le Soir Volé” (The Stolen Soir). In the world’s “first media hack”, a group of Resistance fighters hatch a wild but dangerous plan to print a fake edition of Le Soir, packed with articles mocking the occupier. title: Amazon’s AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 11 Live Feeds on One Screen
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:18am PT Amazon’s AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 11 Live Feeds on One Screen By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Trump White House Pulls Down Tetris-Like Game, in Which You Had to Stop a ‘Zombie Siege’ at Mexican Border, After Company’s Copyright Threat 13 hours ago How Netflix Will Use Apple’s iPhone Duo to Deliver a ‘Big-Screen Feeling’ 17 hours ago Newly Discovered Plant-Eating Insects Named After Taylor Swift 19 hours ago See All Courtesy of AWS Personalized multiview livestreams — the ability to watch multiple video feeds on one screen — have become a popular and much-requested feature by customers, particularly for sports. Now AWS , Amazon ‘s cloud-services division, is launching a new service that will let streamers deliver up to 11 feeds in a single personalized channel. On Thursday, AWS took the wraps off new capabilities in its suite of video services: per-viewer dynamic multiview, AI-generated metadata generation to facilitate monetization opportunities based on what’s happening on screen, and automated backfill of unfilled ad inventory. AWS is showcasing the new capabilities at IBC 2026, running Sept. 11-14 in Amsterdam. Related Stories How 'The Pitt' Production Designer Expanded the Emergency Room for Season 2 Martin Short Gets Honest: What It’s Like to Be All Over the Emmy Race, Thanks to Three Very Different Projects The new capabilities will make it possible to deliver “truly personalized live TV,” said Samira Bakhtiar, general manager of telco, media, entertainment, games and sports at AWS. “AWS helped build the streaming era. Now we’re helping to build the intelligence era. Every frame of live video is personalized and understood.” Popular on Variety The new AWS Elemental MediaPackage Dynamic Multiview lets viewers choose their own multi-camera layout from a single set of encoded sources, delivered to any device over standard HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) or Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) — without per-layout encoding costs India’s JioHotstar is already using the AWS multiview feature to present quad-view features for its coverage of Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket matches. “AWS Elemental MediaPackage Multiview lets us deliver multiple synchronized camera angles within a single stream, putting our subscribers in control of how they experience live sports,” Akash Saxena, CTO of JioHotstar, said in a statement. “The server-side composition approach scales this premium experience to over 100 million viewers without multiplying origin complexity or CDN costs, giving us a true differentiator in India’s competitive OTT landscape.” AWS says that existing approaches to implementing multiview features have forced trade-offs. For example, tiled encoding limits reach to High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC)-capable devices, while client-side compositing demands custom software development kits for each device. Server-side compositing requires pre-encoding every layout combination (each costing as much as a new channel). By contrast, AWS MediaPackage Dynamic Multiview stitches multi-camera and multi-feed layouts on demand from encoded sources, delivered as a single adaptive bitrate stream through HLS or DASH. Sources encode one time through AWS Elemental MediaLive. Then, Elemental MediaPackage assembles layouts in the compressed domain with no reencoding. The output reaches more than 95% of consumer devices with a single digital rights management (DRM) key and requires no SDK, per-device builds, or new vendors, according to AWS. Also being introduced by AWS is Elemental Inference Contextual Metadata, which uses AI to extract metadata from live video in real time. That can then be used to power personalized video experiences and contextual ad decisioning. In addition, the AWS Elemental MediaTailor Yield Optimization capability provides automated backfill of unfilled ad inventory using Amazon Publisher Services (APS) demand, aimed a maximizing ad revenue. The new suite of capabilities also includes AWS Elemental MediaTailor Low-Latency Ad Insertion, which provides personalized ad insertion to low-latency streams using Apple’s HLS interstitials. According to AWS, its cloud services are used by streaming services to nearly 2 billion customers worldwide. Media companies that use AWS include Fox, Amazon MGM Studios, Disney, HBO, NBCUniversal, Sony and Netflix. title: EST N8 Picks Up Manila-Set Crime Thriller ‘Jaguar’ With Elijah Canlas, David Call, Sid Lucero & Gabby Padilla
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Chinese Distributor Hishow Adds ‘Josephine’, ‘Ah Girl’ & ‘Rec’ Franchise To We Love Cinema Release Slate Tokyo Gap Financing Market Unveils 24 Projects & Partnership With Canada’s Frontières Herman Yau’s Audience Award-Winner ‘We’re Nothing At All’ Sold To Blacklight Global For U.S. Release View All September 10, 2026 6:16am Jaguar EST N8 EXCLUSIVE: EST N8 has acquired worldwide rights to Jaguar , a Manila-set crime thriller from director Dean Colin Marcial, a Berlinale Talents Lab alumnus whose work has screened at Toronto, SXSW, Tribeca and Sitges film festivals. The ensemble cast is led by award-winning Filipino actor Elijah Canlas – known for indie breakout hits Kalel, 15 and Sunshine – along with U.S. actor David Call ( Tiny Furniture ; James White ), Sid Lucero (Lav Diaz’s Norte, The End of History ) and Cinemalaya Best Actress winner Gabby Padilla ( Kono Basho ). Also featuring in the cast are Ruby Ruiz, who starred in Prime Video series Expats , Soliman Cruz ( To The North ), Venice best actor winner John Arcilla ( On The Job 2: The Missing 8 ) and Isabel Sandoval ( Lingua Franca ). The film also marks the feature acting debut of Dilaw Obero, the frontman for Filipino rock band Dilaw . Watch on Deadline Related Stories News EST N8 Takes Worldwide Rights To Bangladeshi Rotterdam Winner 'Master' News EST N8 Appoints JP Villanueva As EVP Of Acquisitions & Global Distribution The film follows a young security guard in Manila who accidentally witnesses a high-profile murder involving an American movie star. Described as a combination of Filipino genre cinema with American indie grit, the film explores themes including class, power and corruption. Supported by Purin Pictures and Film London, and winner of the Mocha Chai Laboratories Post-Production Grant at the QCinema Project Market, the film is produced by Braden Friedman ( Little Accidents ), Bam Manlongat ( Under Parallel Skies ) and Marcial. Executive producers include A/Vantage Pictures founder Jason Michael Berman, whose credits include Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest and Ben Affleck’s Air ; Galileo Mondol ( The Creator ) and veteran Filipino producer Moira Lang ( The Blossoming of Maximo Oliveros , Norte, The End of History ). EST N8 will launch international sales on the title at the upcoming Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) Market. The deal for worldwide rights was brokered by Sophie Shi for EST N8, and Bianca Grimshaw with Rebecca Theodore at Granderson Des Rochers LLP on behalf of the filmmakers. “I was just blessed to work with an amazing cast and director that always collaborated to elevate the scenes in the film,” said Canlas, who won several Best Actor awards for his role in Jun Robles Lana’s Kalel, 15 and stood out in Antoinette Jadaone’s social drama Sunshine . “I feel like audiences are craving for unique and fresh ways of telling a story and that’s what we aimed for with Jaguar : a film that follows an ordinary Filipino worker that spirals into unknown territory.” Sophie Changhui Shi, EST N8 Head of Studios, said: “ Jaguar hits the sweet spot for international distributors – it’s an auteur-driven crime story with visceral genre elements and an exceptional festival pedigree that showcases the extraordinary creative energy coming out of Southeast Asian cinema right now.” “Dean Colin Marcial and his team have crafted a story deeply rooted in the local atmosphere while possessing universal tension, further elevating high-concept Asian genre cinema on the world stage. We are thrilled to introduce this raw, electric thriller to global buyers at TIFF.” Marcial noted: “We set out to shoot an incendiary crime story that’s a snapshot of present-day Manila – the bleeding edge of east & west. Sophie and the rest of the EST N8 team share our vision for the film and are champions of the emerging SEA New Wave.” Jason Michael Berman said: “I really believe Jaguar announces Dean as a great new talent. It’s also a genuinely cross-cultural film – pairing a prolific American actor with some of the biggest Filipino stars, and standing as a terrific U.S.-Philippines co-production. “Partnering with the team at EST N8 to launch Jaguar on the international stage at TIFF ensures that this collision of indie filmmaking and Filipino genre reaches the wide global audience it was made for.” The international sales push and global rollout strategy for Jaguar will be led by EST N8 executives Jan Paul Villanueva (EVP, Acquisitions & Global Distribution), Cathy Ni (Head of Sales) and Shams Pasha (Sales & Marketing Executive). EST N8’s TIFF Market slate also inclues B-EST Pictures’ Thai horror debut Tame , Chan Chun-hao’s Taiwanese thriller Dead End , Rezwan Shahriar Sumit’s IFFR Big Screen Award winner Master , and Tetsuya Mariko’s Dear Stranger , starring Hidetoshi Nishijima and Gwei Lun-Mei. Taking place on September 26 in Central Park, they join previously announced performers Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean , Lenny Kravitz, John Legend,Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together. Additionally, Bill Nye, IZA, Jordan Fisher, Katie Couric, Lais Ribeiro, Marcus Samuelsson, Naomi Watanabe, Nomzamo Mbatha, PJ Sin Suela, and Vladimir Duthiers will make appearances, with more names to be announced in the coming weeks. PREVIOUS, August 13: The 2026 Global Citizen Festival in New York’s Central Park next month will feature a line-up including Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean celebrating the 30th anniversary of Fugees’ album The Score, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend, Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey, and Tomorrow X Together. Related Stories Acquisitions Sony Pictures Circling Ridley Scott's 'Treasure Island' Package Starring Hugh Jackman News Hugh Jackman Hopes Next Wolverine Actor "Makes It Their Own": "I'm Not Going To Say Anything" Taking place on Central Park’s Great Lawn on Saturday, September 26, the festival will be hosted by Hugh Jackman , and feature appearances by Rachel Brosnahan and Gayle King, with more to be announced in the coming weeks. Watch on Deadline The line-up was announced today by Global Citizen, considered the world’s largest movement to end extreme poverty. Following the success of the first-ever FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show, which was produced by Global Citizen and helped raise $60 million for the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, this year’s festival will raise awareness for what the organization says are three core issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty across the world. The goals as stated are to create opportunities for 2 million children to go to school, support 1.5 million smallholder farmers, and provide electricity for 2.5 million homes. Tickets to the Global Citizen Festival are free and can be secured by visiting the Global Citizen app and earning points by completing “action journeys” related to the core issues. Points can be redeemed by entering the free ticket lottery or making a $25 charitable donation to instantly secure a ticket. Funds raised will go to New York City’s City Parks Foundation to support their youth education programming and parks initiatives across all five boroughs, as well as to organizations helping those experiencing homelessness across the city. “It’s time to gather once again on the Great Lawn, in the middle of New York City, to tell the world an end to extreme poverty is possible,” said Jackman, Global Citizen Ambassador, in a statement. title: AI Is Deflating Hollywood’s Microdramas Scene
full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:05am China pioneered the microdrama industry as we know it, with the duanju format exploding in popularity during the pandemic. So when AI -generated verticals began flooding the Chinese market and reports emerged that production workers were scared for their jobs, it was an ominous sign for the burgeoning industry in the U.S. Now, it’s become clear that companies serving the American market are very much testing the appeal of these bite-sized, AI-generated stories. Not every firm is going the route of My Muse or Inkitt Ironblood, apps that exclusively release AI verticals, often fantasy, period and action stories that would require some serious budgets if they were filmed in live action. But some major players, including DramaBox, DramaWave and FlareFlow, have increasingly been embracing synthetic actors and settings and showering their apps with prompt-generated, sometimes uncanny fare, no human actors required. For entertainment workers in the Los Angeles area, that shift has come with consequences. In the wake of the 2023 Hollywood strikes, verticals became a lifeline for cast and crew as traditional jobs evaporated. Now, L.A.-based microdrama workers tell The Hollywood Reporter that jobs in the once-reliable industry have become scarcer, while unscrupulous use of the tech on the work of creatives is on the rise. It’s a tough pill to swallow for an underemployed Hollywood workforce that once saw the field as a job-saver. “People who’ve been working full-time in this space for years are going back to their day jobs, going home, and that’s cast, crew, producers,” says Candace Mizga, an actor in the vertical space and co-founder of the microdrama platform Chera TV, which does not use AI. “It has been a huge, huge jump, especially this past couple of months. It’s been pretty wild to see.” It will come as no surprise that AI microdramas can individually be made cheaper, faster and with fewer workers. While budgets for live-action microdramas tend to fall in the $100,000 to $300,000 range, pro-looking, feature-length AI microdramas can cost $60,000 to $100,000, according to AI verticals production studio Axis AI Studios. (Think that’s a bargain? The app TrueShort has claimed its 20- to 30-minute AI projects can be made for as little as $1,000 to $3,000.) In terms of the production schedule, these projects can be completed in two weeks as compared to 12 weeks for a live-action story, per Holywater Tech, which owns the all-AI My Muse app. Owl & Co. And though a live-action shoot might require 50 workers for seven days, “now we would need five people for seven days to make one show,” says Guy Shimoni, the CEO and co-founder of the platform Shortical, which releases both live-action and AI verticals. While microdrama firms have been dipping their toes into AI for some time, the release of the Seedance 2.0 AI video generator tool in February accelerated adoption of the tech, says Shimoni. Once Seedance 2.0 released, enabling that viral video of Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise fighting, “The technology was really there to tell a good story, a good narrative, the art effects weren’t too bad,” Shimoni says. “We all started adopting when Seedance 2.0 came out.” While it’s unclear how much AI is to blame, microdrama insiders say work opportunities at large have recently been slowing. Maddie Grove, a talent manager at LEWK Management, has some 15 actor clients in the verticals space. “June hit and all of a sudden we went from having 15 to 20 different shows casting on breakdowns a day to maybe four,” she says, noting there has been a “significant drop” in employment opportunities. She’s not alone in seeing a larger change afoot. “Last year, I was getting anywhere between five to 15 vertical auditions a week,” says Chera TV co-founder and verticals actor Kylie Karson. “I would say I’m getting two a week [now].” Other cases are more obviously tied to the embrace of the tech. Lucia Lopez is a production designer and director who for half a year worked with a production company in Atlanta to produce a microdrama a month for the platform DramaShorts. The production company’s contract with DramaShorts abruptly ended in July when the company went “fully AI.” She adds, “They don’t want anything as live action. And it was in the blink of an eye.” Now she’s back in L.A. and says outreach to producer contacts hasn’t yielded new work. THR has reached out to DramaShorts for comment. “The sheer speed with which apps have basically shut down entire productions, completely pulled out, completely transitioned over to AI is quite spectacular,” says Jen Cooper, the founder of Vertical Drama Love, a media brand that closely tracks the industry. Still, some companies claim they can create more employment opportunity through AI, not less. Shortical’s Shimoni, who notes that individual AI microdramas might use five employees instead of 50, says platforms can now make many more microdramas, rather than produce the same number with fewer people. He adds, “The business is more efficient. So actually we’re understaffed, we’re recruiting more, we’re missing people.” A makeup artist on the CandyJar microdrama ‘Fight Dirty’ gets star Carter Harvey — who plays a street fighter in the romance series — ready for his close-up during a Los Angeles shoot. The Hollywood Reporter Beyond employment concerns, the rise of AI microdramas has sparked issues for creatives around consent. Vertical actors including Ashley BeLoat and Evan Gambardella spoke to Business Insider in July about platforms allegedly using performances and likenesses from live-action microdramas in fully AI projects without human performers’ permission. The publication also reported on platforms allegedly posting sexualized ads for microdramas that used AI to engineer scenes and dialogue that were never filmed or cleared with the actors involved. Some actors are now negotiating AI language into their contracts. But even for those who have written protections, the paperwork doesn’t always matter. Grove — who is BeLoat, Karson and Mizga’s manager — says that, since June, she’s seen platforms breach actors’ contracts four times when it comes to AI. Sometimes, platforms will hire a third-party ad company with which actors don’t have a contract; that company will “take many creative liberties that are overtly sexual, rage-baiting, clickbaity” for advertisements, Grove adds. Lack of leverage may be one reason why this is happening — companies may bank on the idea that burgeoning performers aren’t going to raise a stink or bankroll expensive lawsuits. But unauthorized use of AI isn’t just impacting niche creatives in the vertical space. Vertical Drama Love’s Cooper and social media users have pointed to the visual similarities between characters in DramaWave’s The Rise of the Lycan Queen and DramaBox’s Deny Me, Dragon King and actor Henry Cavill’s character in The Witcher . Flowing white hair? Check. Broad shoulders? Check. Very square jaw and dark brow? Also check. “I like to play a game of where is Henry,“ wrote one social-media user on Reddit. “Sometimes multiple characters look like him in one drama and they use his witcher voice a lot.” THR has reached out to representatives for Cavill, DramaWave and DramaBox for comment. Unscrupulous use of AI can also affect screenwriters. Writer-actor Tess Dinerstein sold a pirate-themed microdrama script to DramaBox in 2025, before she says AI was on the radar of many companies in the U.S. market. Around the same time as she finished revisions for the drama in 2026, she remembers telling an exec that she wouldn’t like the script being made into an AI show. A few months later, that exec had exited the company, and Dinerstein learned that the show had been released as an AI project. Dinerstein acknowledges that DramaBox owns the full rights to the script, but she won’t watch or publicize the adaptation because she doesn’t approve of it. “When I spend so much time on a script and fall in love with the characters and feel like it could be done really well with people, [the use of AI] takes a lot of the heart and soul out of the piece,” she says. THR has reached out to DramaBox for comment. Where is all this headed? In China, more than 95 percent of microdrama titles in the first three months of 2026 were reportedly made using AI. Across the Pacific, viewer demand will ultimately determine whether AI verticals become a short-term curiosity or a staple of the format. “You have to remember whoever’s running this, they’re running numbers. They don’t care about your face, my face,” says actor Eli Jane, who has appeared in about 30 verticals. “If the audience doesn’t show up for AI, then they’re going to stop making that content.” Worried about the AI invasion, actor Martina Monti — who has some 40 microdramas under her belt — began counting the number of vertical acting jobs posted on the digital casting platform Actors Access in seven-day samples across multiple months to determine if a slowdown was reflected there. (She says it was — Actors Access, which is a go-to platform for microdrama acting jobs, did not respond to a request for data for this story.) Says the performer: “Some people have a more positive expectation for the future. They’re like, ‘Hey, we hope that this AI bubble is going to just pop.’ And other people, we don’t know.” She adds, “It’s not going well for now.” This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: ‘Why Did I Get Married Again?’ Review: Taraji P. Henson Joins the Gang for a Tyler Perry Sequel That Sells the Next Generation Short
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:04am PT ‘Why Did I Get Married Again?’ Review: Taraji P. Henson Joins the Gang for a Tyler Perry Sequel That Sells the Next Generation Short Arriving 16 years after 'Why Did I Get Married Too?,' this Netflix release spends too much time reminding viewers why they should be invested in the franchise. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Company’ Review: Casey Affleck’s Latest Directorial Effort Isn’t What It Initially Appears to Be, but Isn’t Very Interesting Either Way 17 hours ago ‘Bunker’ Review: Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz Are Brilliant in Florian Zeller’s Riveting, Slightly Overstated Thriller of Isolation and Invasion 2 days ago ‘The Spiral’ Review: Paolo Strippoli’s Lurid Faustian Tragedy Shores Up His Reputation as Italy’s New Horror Virtuoso 3 days ago See All ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection It’s been nearly 20 years since “Why Did I Get Married?”, the original Tyler Perry movie that first introduced these characters and their variously troubled relationships — and 16 years since the sequel to that film, “Why Did I Get Married Too?”. So it feels only normal, at the start of this latest outing for the gang, that we should be treated to some fairly heavy exposition. “ Why Did I Get Married Again ?” certainly doesn’t stint on it: As the film begins, we catch up with fiery Angela ( Tasha Smith ) and her husband Marcus ( Michael Jai White ), a now somewhat cowed figure who has quit his womanizing in practice but kept the macho attitude. The pair are preparing to host a dinner ahead of the marriage of their daughter Jasmine (Armani Greer) to football player Wesley (Everett Osborne), who happens to be the son of their friend Roselyn ( Taraji P. Henson , new to the franchise but treated by all and sundry as if she had been part of the adventure all along). Related Stories How Did the Emmys’ Documentary Category Get So Star-Studded? 'Widow's Bay,' 'DTF: St. Louis' and 'Spider-Noir' — Despite Its Cancellation — Dominate Creative Arts Emmys Night 2 Winners (FULL LIST) Tasha and Marcus have of course invited their old friends from the first two films, Shelley (Jill Scott) and Troy (Lamman Rucker), and Diane (Sharon Leal) and Terry (Tyler Perry), who all have children of their own, in their early twenties. Meanwhile, Shelley’s old troublemaker ex, Mike (Richard T. Jones), turns up for some reason, this time dating a much younger woman who happens to be the ex of Angela and Marcus’s son Marcus Jr. (Da’Vinchi). It seems like an overly convoluted set-up — not least because the younger generation don’t bring much to the film apart from narrative developments that reflect the older generation back to them. So, Marcus Jr. is a hot-headed skirt-chaser like his old man, and Diane and Terry fret that their son T.J. (Jaden Michael) may conversely be a little mild. The film is fundamentally uninterested in the younger people as characters, however, which gives it a strange flavor: The kids constantly provide the (rather thin) action, and the older lot then argue, worry or wryly chuckle about these events, saying things like, “Marcus Jr. is just like you used to be, Marcus.” That is to say, the film’s exposition-speak continues long after its opening scenes, permanently relating to the audience what is happening, who is who, and why it concerns the franchise’s veteran characters. That doesn’t make for very enjoyable watching, and it compounds a tonal problem raised by the multi-generational approach: Where the older characters are cheerfully upfront and confrontational about their problems, the younger people have grown up in a world that sees things differently, and therefore appear bland. You have to feel sorry for Marcus Jr., portrayed as the lone bad egg among the dreary new set, whose greatest sin is trying to get with his spoken-for ex-girlfriend a couple of times, only to get a furious dressing-down from Angela in front of everybody. A lightly macho tone prevails, even as Perry writes a handful of quite sensitive scenes for his female characters, such as Shelley’s fears about her aging mother, or Roselyn’s anguish about her son rejecting her. That leads to a curious scene in which Marcus somehow bests the insanely buff Wesley at weightlifting, which seems like nothing so much as wish-fulfillment — and to an even more curious treatment of the character of T.J., who appears to be written as homosexual without this ever being stated. Stranded in a no-man’s land where everybody deplores toxic masculinity but the guys still need to be given something to do, the film doesn’t manage to contrive any actual fun. Popular on Variety Netflix money oozes from every pore of “Why Did I Get Married Again?,” most visibly when the gang head to Lake Como for the nuptials. The ladies duly appear at brunch in a variety of chic ensembles and statement jewelry, and the wedding itself is suitably plush, but all of this merely adds to the film’s strange detachment from reality — an overstuffed chamber-piece with a tenuous connection to actual life and concerns. Among the performers, Smith rules the roost as the no-nonsense Angela, and Jones acquits himself tolerably on comic relief duties as the pathetic Mike. Henson, apparently acting in another film entirely, gives us a character unable to submit to true love in the face of her perceived duties; alone of all the actors, she gets close to something truthful, but that still sits quite uncomfortably with the ambient tone of woolly half-jokes and that’s-life sermonizing. That spirit finds its most naked expression in a drably conceived scene toward the film’s conclusion, in which the older characters gather in a semi-circle to literally explain everything to the younger generation (who are also seated in a semi-circle). Everybody takes turns to speak their hard truth or life lesson or warm expression of love. A wedding dance scene — interspersed with bloopers to remind you that you have been watching a comedy — caps off proceedings with something like relief, the assignment finally completed. ‘Why Did I Get Married Again?’ Review: Taraji P. title: Monica Dolan Shares How She Prepared to Portray the Woman Who Uncovered an Irish Mass Grave Scandal in ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’: TIFF
full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 10, 2026 6:01am Monica Dolan in 'The Lost Children of Tuam' Courtesy of Element Pictures Monica Dolan ( Mr Bates vs The Post Office , Pride , Wolf Hall , Black Mirror ) is quietly having a banner year. At the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), the English character actress is pulling triple duty, appearing in no fewer than three films. In the real-life The Lost Children of Tuam , produced by Liam Neeson and directed by Frank Berry, Dolan stars as history enthusiast Catherine Corless, who researched the Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home in Tuam, Ireland, only to uncover that as many as 796 children had been buried in unmarked graves on the property. The movie world-premiered at the Galway Film Fleadh in July, where it won the best Irish film award, and will screen in the Centerpiece Program at Toronto, beginning on Sunday, Sept. 13. Related Stories Movies Oscars: Australia Picks 'First Light' as International Feature Contender (Exclusive) TV 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' Dropped by BBC Also at Toronto, you can see Dolan in the world premiere of John Madden’s Onwards and Sideways , starring Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans as two people with a lot in common – a great sense of humor, a love of dance, and, as just diagnosed, Parkinson’s. Dolan plays the sister of Ifans’ character. And then there is Simon Stone’s Elsinore , which is already attracting awards season buzz after its Venice world premiere before it heads to Toronto. Starring Andrew Scott as British actor Ian Charleson, who throws himself into playing Hamlet while succumbing to AIDS, the film’s ensemble cast features Dolan as the sarcastic receptionist at the National Theatre in London. If you needed any more proof of Dolan’s versatility, earlier this year, she also featured in the supporting cast of season 2 of BBC comedy series Smoggie Queens . Her role: the ex-wife of the drag queen character Mam, played by Mark Benton. Dolan studied drama at the Guildhall School in London and then went into television, soon turning heads, including with characters who have darker sides. Among others, she played a real-life stalker in U Be Dead and serial killer Rosemary West in Appropriate Adult opposite Dominic West, a role for which she won the BAFTA TV Award. More recently, she drew praise, nominations and awards for her portrayal of a real-life woman in charge of a local post office branch in ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office . You may also remember her for portraying George Mackay’s bigoted mother in the 2014 film Pride . On stage, she won the 2019 Laurence Olivier Award for best supporting actress for playing Karen Richards in the West End production of All About Eve . Rhys Ifans and Monica Dolan in ‘Onwards and Sideways’ Courtesy of BBC/Hilltop Screen Dolan talked to THR about her TIFF films, needing a coach to nail the right Irish regional accent in The Lost Children of Tuam despite having Irish parents, how she chooses roles, and why she likes to explore a wide range of human behavior. How does it feel to have three films at the Toronto festival? Or is this something you do regularly? (laughs) No, I’ve never had this before. It is really incredible. Actually, I was very, very excited when I heard I’d got two, and my agent and I were trying to organize all the logistics. And then I just got another little one-line email saying, “By the way, Elsinore is in there as well.” But really luckily, they all fall over the same weekend, so I can be there for all three. I’m really happy about that. In The Lost Children of Tuam , you are the protagonist, while in the other two films, you’re part of great ensembles. Is the work much different for you when leading a project? Yes, they’re quite different skills. I’m quite lucky in that I’ve played lots of lead roles in the theater, and when you do that, you’re leading the whole company for quite a long time. It is sort of a marathon rather than a sprint. But when you’re in an ensemble, the important thing to remember, always, is that you’re telling a story. And when you’re in an ensemble, part of your job is to support and just to treat that seriously. It’s quite uncommon for me to lead a film, but I absolutely love the experience, and I’ve been watching other leading actors closely. So, hopefully, I didn’t make too much of a mess of it. Well, I didn’t know Catherine Corless before The Lost Children of Tuam , but I was captivated by her as portrayed by you. Did you get to spend much time with her in preparing for the role and what did you look for? I was really, really lucky with Catherine because she’s a beautiful person. She’s incredibly approachable, and she just thinks in a very unusual way. If I asked off-the-wall questions at whatever time of day or night, it never really fazed her. I might go from asking something very specific about maps and death certificates to saying, “Do you wear your jewelry at night?” Because you’re creating a whole person. She was really wonderful. I visited their small [agricultural] holding. I met Aidan, Catherine’s husband. I met their dogs. And I met some of her family, and I was there when the cows ran into the garden, so that was fun. Catherine also made a physical model of the Mother and Baby Home. There were so few photographs, and she wanted to be able to visualize it. And she wanted the survivors to be able to visualize it as well. So she showed me that and talked me through that. That was quite illuminating. Once I started talking to her about the model, everything became a bit more three-dimensional. And I realized that I actually just wanted to know what she cared about and what was important to her. And they got a wonderful field at the back, and we went for a walk around there, and I think maybe that was my most valuable time with her. Information about herself just flowed more freely, and it was also more two-way because I was talking about myself as well. I think we went on the walk because I asked, “What’s your favorite thing?” and she said, “my garden.” So I got a real sense of what she really cares about. I don’t think I’ve met anyone who has more care and value and love for living things. Monica Dolan in ‘Mr Bates vs the Post Office,’ courtesy of ITV PBS/ITV/Masterpiece Theatre / Courtesy Everett Collection That’s fascinating! Are there any things you always ask when portraying a real-life person? One thing that I’ve developed, which I’ve found really useful, is to ask the person, if it is a real person, and if they don’t mind – I wouldn’t ask everyone – to record just 15 minutes of their life story. What’s really good about that is that you get their voice and you get their background in one. And if it is about 15 minutes, you can listen to it on your way from the unit base to the set. Also, if you’re asking somebody to tell you about themselves, they’re not thinking about their voice as much. If you’re asking them something that they know a lot about, and they can hopefully get involved in, and they’re obviously emotionally involved in because it’s themselves, they [don’t think and worry too much] about their voice. How else do you get into a character, especially when she is not based on a real-life person? We also had a really terrific script here. Rebecca Lenkiewicz ( She Said , Ida ) spent a lot of time with Catherine. It might sound like quite a radical thing to say, but most of the time when I’m reading a script, I mainly look at the behavior of the people and not really at what they’re saying. One of the characters I played actually was at her most chatty when she was about to do something really awful, but didn’t say very much otherwise. If I were speaking to younger people at drama school, I think I’d tell them that as a tip – to look at the character’s behavior. Catherine, early on, really found it very hard to believe that once people knew the truth, they wouldn’t act on it. She spends a lot of the film being quite bewildered, and she did spend a lot of her time being quite bewildered about that in real life. She realizes that they’re purposely ignoring her, and that creates an enormous amount of anger and depression. With anything where you’re pursuing a cause or request, most of the time the person or the character has something that makes them very personally invested. I think that in her darkest moments, that was what kept her going. Catherine did speak to me about her relationship with her mother, and their relationship wasn’t the easiest. After her death, Catherine and her husband researched her mother’s background and discovered that she was illegitimate [and had been raised by foster families]. So, it’s about her personal motivation and also how she’s trying to do the right thing, while it’s becoming really apparent that nobody else is. I think she’s an extraordinary woman in that. I think other people, practically anybody else, could have had all of the information that she had, but wouldn’t have been able to put it together in the way that she did and wouldn’t have been able to even notice what she did notice. Gillian Anderson and Monica Dolan in ‘All About Eve’ Jan Versweyveld I read that your parents are Irish. Could you tap into their Irish for the role of Catherine? My mum’s from Enniscorthy in County Wexford, and my dad’s from Swords in Dublin, neither of which accents [is from] the West of Ireland, so I sort of had to start from scratch. I had a really wonderful coach, Paul. Why did you become an actress in the first place? I’ve always been quite nosy and sort of gossipy. You must have that as a journalist as well. (laughs) So, I like doing detective work about people. I don’t always notice it at the time, but I realize it later. I think it’s partly because I was the youngest of four, and I was five years younger than the next one up. So I needed to do quite a bit of showing off to get any attention. Everyone else was very academic and very clever in my family. With acting, you can behave in the most extreme and appalling and exciting ways, and there aren’t any consequences because it’s all a game. I mean, hopefully there are not any personal consequences, but you’re sometimes dealing with quite extreme things. You’re exploring sides of human nature and putting yourself in someone else’s skin, experiencing that. I think it creates more empathy in oneself. And I’d go as far as to say I’ve definitely learnt from each of the characters I’ve played, and hopefully they sort of stretch you as a person. You’ve played some really dark and scary characters in dramas, and then I saw you earlier this year in the BBC comedy Smoggie Queens , about the chosen family and lives of a group of LGBTQ+ friends. How do you choose roles, or how did that comedy role come about? A lot of it depends on what I’m offered. With Smoggie Queens , I saw the first [season] and I absolutely loved it. My friend Mark Benton, who I’ve known for years, was in it playing Mam. So, I texted him and said, “Oh my gosh, I love this series. If there’s ever a part for me, can you let me know?” And so, then, in the next [season], I was playing his ex-wife Paula. That group of people and that production is incredibly well organized and incredibly humane and enormous fun. It was just wonderful being around those people. They are so big-hearted and witty. At this stage in your career, do you have any preference for film, TV or theater? The atmosphere and the production on every series and every film will be different. And the dynamic of every production is different, be it theater, film or television. I really enjoy variety. THR

title: Musical ‘& Juliet’ Will End Broadway Run In January
full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:00am The Broadway production of '& Juliet.' Matthew Murphy Musical & Juliet will end its Broadway run in January, after more than four years on Broadway. The show, created by David West Read, reimagines the Shakespearean tragedy so that Juliet lives and is set to a pop score from Max Martin, with songs including “Since U Been Gone,” “Roar,” and “I Want It That Way.” The musical, which is set to close Jan. 3, 2027, is the last remaining show on Broadway from the 2022-2023 season. The show began in the UK before opening on Broadway at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre on November 17, 2022. The Broadway musical recouped its $17 million capitalization in 2024 (and the tour recouped in 2025), and has since grossed more than $175 million. Though capacity has remained fairly strong throughout its run, grosses have begun to trend downward over the past two years. It joins Six , another longer running musical which opened in 2021, in announcing a January closing date. Related Stories Lifestyle Broadway Box Office: 'Hamilton' Leads Labor Day Weekend Grosses Lifestyle Scott Rudin Plans Two New Broadway Shows, Including One With Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd Throughout its run, the musical has welcomed a number of celebrities making their Broadway debuts, including Chrissy Metz and Joey Fatone, both currently in the cast, as well as Charli D’Amelio, Laurie Hernandez, Kandi Burruss and Cheryl Porter. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson also had a one-night, walk-on role in the musical. Before the show ends on Broadway run, it will welcome Kenzie Ziegler, Aly Michalka, Spencer Sutherland, Anthony Gargiula and more. The musical is produced on Broadway by Max Martin, Tim Headington, Theresa Steele Page, Jenny Petersson, Martin Dodd and Eva Price. THR

title: Anchor Access, Original Shows and a Real-Life Lounge: Inside MS NOW’s Membership Push
full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 6:00am A rendering of the MS NOW Members Lounge in Dallas MS NOW Latr this month a few thouand of MS NOW ‘s biggest fans will descend on College Park Center at the University of Texas at Arlington for what the news brand says will be its biggest event yet: “MS NOW Live: Together in Texas.” The event comes at a critical moment for MS NOW, which this week launched its first subscription offering, the MS NOW membership. The Texas event, it turns out, will be a testing ground, in more ways than one. MS NOW members attending the live event will discover a dedicated members lounge, with a bar, comfortable seating, and the opportunity to mingle with other super fans as well as some of the channel’s talent. “As a long timer in our business, I feel like it’s really, really different,” says Marcus Mabry, MS NOW’s senior VP of content strategy, “I’ve never had anything like this in any other news space I’ve been in, we actually want to emphasize people being together, and that’s really powerful.” “We’ve ignored humanity for some reason,” he adds. “So even down to the decor, the offerings of food and beverage, even down to that, it’s about warmth and celebration, and it celebrates of our democracy, which we don’t often do that much these days in our country.” Mabry says that MS NOW intends to pop up member lounges throughout the year, likely tied to live MS NOW events or news events, a real-life benefit to a digital subscription, and one of many features that executives at the cable channel hope will help it stand out in a crowded space for subscriptions. “Our challenge is to prove to our audience, which is many million strong, that this is worth their time and this is worth their wallet, and we are pretty humble about the task in front of us, and we know that it’s a busy, crowded marketplace,” MS NOW president Rebecca Kutler says, when asked by The Hollywood Reporter in the company’s New York headquarters about entering a crowded market. “We think through our research that we have found a white space that’s meaningful. We think we are creating something that doesn’t currently exist, and now it’s on our team to deliver on that and earn, earn our members, earn the community.” The membersip will have plenty of video content, of course. All the MS NOW shows are there, as are a slate of originals, including interview programs hosted by Rachel Maddow and Claire McCaskill, a data-centric program led by Ali Velshi, The Very Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell, and a legal show led by Andrew Weissmann. But the company is leaning into the other stuff even more: Live Q&A’s with anchors and correspondents, twice per day, including standing Q&A’s every week with the likes of Rachel Maddow and Joe Scarborough. The talent has fully bought in. “For us on the talent side, we all raised our hands because we also know what the future looks like, right?” says Stephanie Ruhle, who will also do weekly Q&As. “This wasn’t a question of, do we want to enter into a new venture with Rebecca? We make great shows and we feel great about it, but it’s not a secret that linear TV is going in one direction, and so none of us are saying, ‘well, we’re going to jump off this ship.’ We’re saying we are part of an amazing machine. We see where the future is. Why don’t we maintain what we have and now jump into this new venture? That’s not a giant financial investment for our company, that’s an investment for all of us in our collective futures.” There will be news, but not too much news, and at the end of the day’s top stories, there will be a dedicated mindfulness experience, in partnership with Calm. In their research, executives found that consumers “said they were overwhelmed by the sheer volume of news. They said they were isolated, either because they were blue dots in red states, or because they were afraid to wade into the cesspool that is social media. And they told us they were anxious, either about the state of the country, or the state of the world, or frankly the future of our democracy,” says Mabry. “So what we’ve done in the MS NOW membership and app is we’ve built a product designed to confront overwhelm with concise curation, to defeat isolation with connection, both to our journalists and to each other, and to confront anxiety by giving our members agency,” he adds. “I don’t know whose idea was to put wellness into this thing, but it’s brilliant because that is literally the antidote to everything I hear,” quips Velshi, speaking to reporters in MS NOW’s office this week. The mindfulness content will include meditation exercises, but also content from doctors, therapists and psychologists, not to mention former ABC News correspondent Dan Harris, who left ABC five years ago to focus on his meditation company. “I think there’s a huge opportunity here, and there’s a real service that can be provided,” Harris says. “A lot of people feel like they need their anxiety and anger in order to do anything in this environment, and I get that. I’m not trying to deny you your anger, I just don’t think it’s the cleanest burning fuel. I think the cleanest burning fuel is a regulated nervous system that allows you to respond wisely with maximum effectiveness.” But getting together in real life will be a big piece of it, through big events, members lounges, and even live tapings of episodes like The Weeknight, which will also be heading to Texas. “I think this is actually very transformative,” says Weeknight co-host Symone Sanders. “It is no small thing that a news organization, especially in this economy, is investing in their folks going on the road, but also investing in in-person experiences. It feels kind of BravoCon-ish, if you will.” “It is building on the connections, the parasocial relationship, frankly, that we build with our audience for the people that tune in with us every night. But I think this kind of investment is the future, and we’ve clearly got something going,” she continued. “We are inviting people to our table, and so we want folks to feel like they are literally sitting down having dinner with us every night. And the in-person aspect of that just allows us to magnify it even more.” If CNN’s subscription is for news junkies, and Fox Nation is for Fox fans, MS NOW thinks it can carve out a slice of the business that is distinct, and less dependent on a linear TV brand that is sliding in one direction. “We believe, and you’ll hear me say this over and over again, our brand is to be pro-democracy, and if you are pro-democracy, kind of subhead A of that is strong, free, and fair press, and that is a huge part of what we are building, both for our DTC community and for the overall MS NOW brand,” Kutler says. . THR

title: Belmont Cameli and NHL Phenom Macklin Celebrini Talk ‘Off Campus,’ Olympic Heartbreak and Handling the Hype
full_text: Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close Macklin Celebrini (left) and Belmont Cameli were photographed Aug. 17 in Vancouver. Cameli styling by Sydney Lopez. On Cameli: Saint Laurent shirt, pants; Calvin Klein tank; IWC watch; Jack Spade belt. Celebrini styling by Courtney Mays. On Celebrini: Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee. Photographed by Amanda Pratt; Cameli hair: Rexford Bangle; Celebrini grooming: Erin Klassen; Fashion assistants: Bea Crane and Tallulah Crane “I’m not a hockey player, but I play one on TV,” could be the calling card for several of today’s hottest young actors. Belmont Cameli , the 28-year-old star of Prime Video’s Off Campus , falls into that group — but more impressive is how quickly he’s distinguished himself within it. Ask any Hollywood casting director to name the top up-and-coming talents, and Cameli will almost certainly be near the top of that list. Still, playing a sexy hockey player on TV and being an actual player in the NHL are very different jobs, performed by very different types of guys. That’s what we assumed, anyway, when we brought together Cameli and Macklin Celebrini , the San Jose Sharks’ wunderkind center, for THR ‘s Game Recognize Game video series. As their conversation reveals, the pair have a lot more in common than we could have expected. Related Stories Lifestyle Sydney Sweeney Stars in Provocative Ad Campaign for Novig Sports Trading App THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue The Athlete Is the Studio On Cameli: Saint Laurent shirt, pants; Calvin Klein tank; IWC watch; Jack Spade belt. On Celebrini: Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee. Photographed by Amanda Pratt Of course, we did know that both are in the midst of meteoric rises. Off Campus is hardly Cameli’s first project — the Chicago-area native has worked alongside Robert De Niro and was a series regular on the Saved by the Bell reboot — but his role as college hockey star Garrett Graham has completely changed his career trajectory. He’s currently shooting the show’s second season in Vancouver. Celebrini also has been spending his summer in his hometown of Vancouver, much of it at a training rink. Only 20, Celebrini is already a bona fide NHL superstar. He earned his first Olympic medal this year, winning silver with Team Canada after falling to the U.S. in the gold medal game. And in July, he inked a five-year, $94 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid player in the league at the time (a one-of-a-kind version of his rookie trading card recently sold for $1.28 million at auction). While this is the first time Cameli and Celebrini have met, they had a previous close call. Celebrini was asked to make a cameo appearance in Off Campus . “Can you tell me why the shoot time was from midnight until 3 a.m.?” asks Celebrini, jokingly incredulous. Learning about the brutal production schedule of an actor has him wondering whether he actually has it easy. Cameli is quick to set him straight: “Nobody’s hitting me at full speed.” “Every day, there are kids around watching the practice,” says Celebrini. “They want their stuff signed, and for me that’s really cool because I was that kid hanging around.” Won Hundred shirt; Madewell tee; Our Legacy track pants; Celebrini’s necklace. Photographed by Amanda Pratt “I ALWAYS BELIEVED THAT I COULD SORT IT OUT” BELMONT CAMELI Do you know that we share a common trainer? Barb [Underhill]. MACKLIN CELEBRINI She’s teaching you how to skate? She’s great. CAMELI We came here for two weeks in March for a boot camp during the offseason, and that’s when we met Barb. We have a few mutual friends, actually, because you know [New York Rangers defenseman] Vincent Iorio. CELEBRINI He’s your double. I played with Vinny on the San Jose Sharks for a couple of months. CAMELI I want to ask you the same question I like to ask anyone who plays hockey. What’s the greatest in-game moment you’ve ever had? CELEBRINI Stepping onto the ice at the Olympics was one of the coolest things I’ve ever done. Representing Canada, knowing how global that is and how big that tournament is. That was one of the most special moments for me. CAMELI I feel that when we’re shooting, and I got the Garrett Graham jersey on, I step out and it’s a mostly empty rink that they will fill in with fans later with special effects. ( Laughs .) It’s kind of something like that. Maybe not completely. CELEBRINI Very similar. Lots of cameras. CAMELI What is something people constantly assume about you that is completely wrong? CELEBRINI I think hockey players in general have a bad rap of not having much personality. It’s just what the culture has always been with hockey, but if you meet some of the guys that play in the NHL, they’re some of the funniest guys. I feel like that really doesn’t get portrayed very well on camera. CAMELI There’s something about the locker room interviews in hockey that are pretty fucking serious. We have tons of doubles who’ve grown up playing hockey and they are a bunch of goofballs. You were drafted first overall. What was draft day like? CELEBRINI I thought I was going to be super nervous and a little panicked. You walk up in front of all those people, and it’s a real raw moment for you. The thing that surprised me most was that I was very calm. When I got picked, it was more exciting than anything. Mine was at the Las Vegas Sphere. It was such a big production that I think it was one of the coolest drafts that they’ve had. CAMELI When did you start playing hockey? How old were you? CELEBRINI I was 3 years old when I put on skates and started skating around the rink. Not long after, I started playing hockey. CAMELI I was 27. CELEBRINI Really? You were 27 when you started acting? CAMELI No, when I started skating. ( Laughs. ) I was 20 or 21 when I started acting. I hadn’t been a performer. I was an athlete before that. I played football, wrestling and volleyball. When you were a kid, was your dream always to go to the NHL? CELEBRINI That was always my dream. Growing up here, watching the NHL all the time, put it in my head that it was bigger than something that I could do. I was just dreaming about it. When did you know you could act professionally? For sports , it’s a little bit easier because you see all the guys you’re playing against and there’s rankings. “You can say whatever you want about me or people in my life, but it’s not going to affect me because I’m fully aware of what my reality looks like and feels like,” says Cameli. Saint Laurent shirt, pants, loafers; Calvin Klein tank; Maor ring; Cameli’s necklace; IWC watch; Wander socks; Jack Spade belt. Photographed by Amanda Pratt CAMELI Full honesty, I thought I could act professionally before I ever acted. I was a college student and was studying business. I realized that’s not what I wanted. I arrived very quickly at the dream of being a filmmaker. I hadn’t done it before, but I thought I could figure that out. I didn’t know for certain that I would have success, and I imagined it would take quite some time, but I always believed that I could sort it out. But the first time I actually felt like a professional actor was when I shot a horror film in Budapest. It was a really fun shoot for a movie called Until Dawn , which was based on a video game. When was the first inkling that you could get drafted and could compete in the NHL? CELEBRINI I did a lot of interviews from when I was 14 and on. The biggest question was if I thought about playing in the NHL one day. My answer was always that I didn’t think about it very much because I was trying to focus on what I was doing. Obviously, I thought about it. I watched NHL games and dreamed of playing in the league and achieving that goal. But I think juniors — I was 16, so two years back from my draft year — was the first time I started thinking I could actually play in the NHL. CAMELI How old were you when you got drafted? CELEBRINI I turned 18 on June 13, and then the draft was June 30. I played my first NHL game three months later. That summer was insane. It moved so fast. Photographed by Amanda Pratt “NOBODY IS KNOCKING ME OFF MY FEET” CELEBRINI Have you ever had to cry on set? How do you make yourself cry? CAMELI Yes, I’ve had to cry on set. The thing about Off Campus is that it gets pretty heavy. We deal with some pretty serious themes. For me, I don’t have a real good hack beyond the text, so if the script is written emotionally enough, it’ll move me. Some people are better at it than others. There are some actors on this show who are just like, boom. I’m not there. I need to believe it. CELEBRINI Your shoot days are 14 hours sometimes. Do you get coffee or do you do something else to kind of get you through? CAMELI Last year, Ella [Bright] and I were really working close to 80 hours every single week, so when I have big full weeks like that, it’s no coffee in the morning. I’ll probably end up with one or two coffees in a day, but I don’t do the first one until hours into the day. If I start with it right away, I’m going to need another one in two hours. Then I’ll end up having five or six more. Sugar-free Red Bulls are popular on our set. You were almost on our show, right? CELEBRINI Yeah. Can you tell me why the shoot time was from midnight until 3 a.m.? Would that be on a Saturday or what? It was an absurd time to film. CAMELI There is no absurd time to film. You could be filming at any given moment. CELEBRINI Talking about how long your days are, I think being an athlete’s pretty easy. It might be the best job in the world. CAMELI Yeah, but nobody’s knocking me off my feet and hitting me full speed. CELEBRINI That’s true, you could get hurt. CAMELI What does your offseason regimen look like? Is it up to you? Are you designing it? CELEBRINI My dad specializes in sports medicine and science. For the past eight years, he’s worked with the Golden State Warriors. I also have a strength and conditioning coach that my dad worked really closely with, so they put their heads together and come up with a program based on whatever I feel like I need to work on and get better at. I trust them. CAMELI Are you on a pretty strict diet? CELEBRINI I try to eat as good as I can. Obviously, I cheat on it a little bit. Throughout the week, it’s more [about the] routine. In the morning, I’ll make eggs and sourdough toast. I bring a smoothie with me, so I always have something. The days are long. I usually get the same stuff because it’s routine, and I like it. It’s healthy. CAMELI What part of your game are you most focused on getting better and growing over your offseason this year? CELEBRINI Last year, with the Olympics, we played a lot of games. It was the first year where I played way more games than I practiced. In the second half of the year, I didn’t really skate unless it was a game, which was the weirdest thing ever. I’d get off the ice, and I wouldn’t touch the ice until warm-ups of the next game. It was [about] energy. You just don’t have enough energy to even get dressed and get out there. It takes a lot. Especially after the Olympics, that kind of drained you a little bit. That impacts my top speed. CAMELI What’s your top speed? CELEBRINI Last year, I think it was like 22 miles an hour, 21, 20 something. I feel like I got caught, especially with how many games I played. It was tough to feel fresh every night. I’m balancing some of that conditioning with speed work and trying to get faster and have a little bit more pop. CAMELI What I love about hockey is how individual it is in play style. I’m still developing mine. CELEBRINI If this show runs for 10 seasons, you’re going to get real good. Photographed by Amanda Pratt CAMELI The best thing that would help my game right now is being able to transition from skating forwards to backwards and backwards to forwards while having some speed. Not quite there yet. And stopping. I can skate so fast, but I can’t stop so good. I hit the boards at least once a day. At full speed. CELEBRINI Get Barb on that. That should be the first thing. Starting and stopping. CAMELI I can stop on my right pretty good, but I don’t even really have the left at all. Sometimes we’re shooting, and for the camera, I have to do it on the left side. I’m like, “You guys have to move the camera to the other side because I can’t do that.” I want to ask you about the Olympics. In four years when you win, we’ll do this again. What was it like? You’ve lost other big games, but how did you deal? CELEBRINI Obviously, because of the magnitude of the game — USA and Canada, that rivalry, and then the history that went into it. I don’t know if you saw it, but I had a lot of chances in that game. I had a breakaway. I had a couple chances. Their goalie played unbelievably. [When it comes to losing,] I have a very short memory because I’m not really thinking about anything except for what I’m doing. I forget to text people back. It’s just the way I am. Honestly, I haven’t watched the game back. I can’t really let it eat at me just because in two years we have the World Cup of hockey and then another Olympics. CAMELI Is there a part of you using it as fuel? CELEBRINI That’s the way a lot of people have brought it to me, but you may never get that opportunity again. When COVID happened, NHL players weren’t in the Olympics, and also there was a lockout that made the NHL players not play in the Olympics. For 12 years, those guys that would’ve played in the Olympics didn’t get the chance. You never know what’s going to happen. I think about it all the time. I wish there was a better outcome, but to your point, there’s a reason for everything that happens. I’m a big believer in that. There was some stuff to learn from that. It’s like, you do a lot of auditions, how did you handle hearing “no”? CAMELI You can’t really let the “no” affect you because it’s just part of the job. My real job is to procure more work. The job happens when I’m at home shooting self-tapes, memorizing lines, reading scripts, building out characters for auditions. You hear “no” on most of those. “THERE’S ANOTHER LEVEL TO FANDOM THESE DAYS” CAMELI Hype is interesting. You went No. 1 overall, you’re leading the team down there in San Jose. You probably started getting attention pretty young. CELEBRINI Hockey’s a little different than other sports in that way. There’s attention around you, but some of the top basketball prospects or football prospects, there are cameras at every high school game. It’s just a different level. I didn’t have that very much. Then you just kind of get used to it. People are always talking about you, and you can’t really pay attention to it because there are so many opinions out there that don’t matter. CAMELI Especially in sports. You get people critiquing your game, and then on and off the ice. It’s kind of the same with us, too. Being an actor, everybody has something to say about your performance, but then they also have everything to say about what’s happening in your personal life, too. CELEBRINI I feel like that’s a big thing for actors. Do you feel like people are too invested in your personal life? How do you feel about that? Do you have paparazzi following you around? CAMELI There’s been some paps around. That’s all new and kind of strange. Look, if you’re a fan of the show — the thing that I’m so proud of and pour my heart and soul into — then that’s fucking awesome. But the way our show popped, there’s another level to fandom these days, especially with the internet. Sometimes there’s a real venom to the way people put you under microscopes. You feel constantly observed. I’ve been pretty good with handling that. You can say whatever you want about me or people in my life, but it’s not going to affect me because I’m fully aware of what my reality looks like and feels like. A lot of people have really nice things to say, and a lot of people have mean things to say. To me, it’s just all noise. When I see people out, and they come up to say they love the show, that’s always really enjoyable. It doesn’t always go that way. Some people will just run up with a camera in your face and ask for a picture. I’ll be like, “No, hello?” People get excited. Usually, they’re really sweet. What about you? Photographed by Amanda Pratt CELEBRINI While you were talking, I was relating to everything you were saying. Maybe not as much as you, but it’s a different feeling when it’s kids or the people who look up to you. I get that a lot with younger kids around the rink. Usually, every summer I skate at a private rink, but this summer I’ve been skating at a very public rink. Every day, there are kids around watching the practice. They want their stuff signed, and for me that’s really cool because I was that kid hanging around. My dad worked for the Canucks for four years, so I was around some of the professional players. I know how much it meant to me. That’s something that I’ll never really get sick of. But there are some incidents where it gets a little weird. CAMELI Have you ever searched your own name? CELEBRINI I have. Just to see what’s going on. I can’t say I do it very much, but I have done it before. CAMELI Check the temperature. I’ve done it before, too. Right when we started to do press for this show and the noise started up, I did it. It was mostly good and some bad. I haven’t done it since. I’m really protective of making sure that the choices I make, the things that I do and the people I surround myself with are things that serve me. That type of thing doesn’t always accomplish that task. You signed a new contract lately. What was that for? CELEBRINI Five years, $18.8 million a year, $94 million total. CAMELI What was that like for you when you signed that big contract? CELEBRINI It was exciting. The entry-level contracts in the NHL aren’t quite as big as other sports, so this is the first time you make real money. Well, in terms of professional sports. Obviously, a million dollars a year is a lot of money. In terms of the actual contract, it still feels weird because that’s not really why I’m playing. It was a long negotiation trying to figure out what worked best for our young team. Making sure everyone gets paid and where the [salary] cap is going. [It was] figuring out all that data and figuring out what makes the most sense, and we landed on that. CAMELI Has your spending gone up? CELEBRINI No. I mean, it’s been a couple weeks. CAMELI No, me neither. What’s the first big thing you want to buy? Boat? House? Houseboat? CELEBRINI A houseboat would be great. That’d be awesome. Probably a house. I don’t really need anything else. CAMELI I’m there too, honestly. I still have the same closet of clothes. I probably will still have that same wardrobe for a long time. I drive my Honda, the first car I bought. I’ll drive that puppy until the wheels fall off. Having opportunities to make a good living, doing what I love doing, I’ll never take that for granted. I’m just grateful to be in a greater position to help other people. CELEBRINI Did you get a bump from season one to season two? CAMELI Yeah. When you sign an X amount of years for a TV show, there’s one baked in there. It’s commonplace to renegotiate at a certain point. CELEBRINI How many seasons do you think Off Campus will run for? CAMELI That’s a question that, from you, I really like. From a journalist, I’d be like, “You’re trying to dig.” My business answer is Amazon optioned all the books a couple of years ago. There are five books in the first [series]. There are another four [in the second series]. In success, it could run for a long time. We all hope so. Does the kind of money you’re making add pressure? CELEBRINI It’s cliché, but I have expectations for myself with the way I prepare and how much confidence and belief I have in myself. I want to do as good as anyone else wants me to do. I already put that pressure on myself to perform. [We went] into last year with higher expectations on our team, and then going into this year with higher expectations on our team — it’s just going to keep building. But it doesn’t really change what we do on the ice. I’m never going to change what I do because of outside circumstances. That doesn’t affect the game at all. This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s September 2026 Sports issue .

title: James Marcus Haney’s ‘Black Sunflowers’ Boarded by Charades and CAA Media Finance Ahead of TIFF Docs Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:00am PT James Marcus Haney’s ‘Black Sunflowers’ Boarded by Charades and CAA Media Finance Ahead of TIFF Docs Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Sean Penn is an executive producer on "Black Sunflowers," a documentary feature portraying Ukrainian youths. By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie ‘Red Rocks’ Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago ‘Call My Agent! The Movie’ Premieres in Paris as Ted Sarandos Touts Netflix’s ‘Vital’ Role in France Amid Regulatory Fight 21 hours ago Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Charades Charades and CAA Media Finance are launching sales on “ Black Sunflowers ,” the timely new feature documentary directed by James Marcus Haney (“No Cameras Allowed”) which will premiere at Toronto. Slated to premiere in the TIFF Docs section, “Black Sunflowers” portrays a young generation of Ukrainians, soldiers and civilians, whose coming of age is shaped by martial law and duty on the front lines. As another year of conflict stretches on, Haney captures the ordinary moments amid the war, moving between fast cars, underground clubs and conversations about the future. Related Stories French Drama Series 'The Red and the Black': Passion, Power, Political Intrigue and Victor Belmondo’s Anti-Romantic Hero Underwater Life Breaks New Comedy Ground in 'Submarine Jim,' Xilam's Latest Animated IP The American filmmaker closely collaborated with a Ukrainian production team led by Volodymyr Yatsenko at Limelite (“To the Victory!”), alongside a local crew. Popular on Variety The film is produced by Pedram Rezaee and Vlad Bolyelov and co-produced by Yevhenii Zdorovylo, Samy Mosher, Eric Maldin, Volodymyr Yatsenko and Anna Yatsenko, with Mikayla Jean Miller serving as creative producer. Sean Penn has joined the film as an executive producer, alongside Jay and Cameron Bush, Adam Tudhope, Anna October and Dianna Agron. Charades handles international sales and co-reps North America and global rights with CAA Media Finance. The film boasts a powerful soundtrack with music from British record producer Fred again.. and Brian Eno’s Secret Life project, as well as an original score by Brad Oberhofer and Ukrainian electronic composer Koloah. Also featured in the soundtrack are Aphex Twin, Four Tet, Idles, Sega Bodega, Nastya Vogan, Два Два Дев’ять, Ann Annie and Morwan. The film closes with a version of Morphine’s “Do Not Go Quietly Unto Your Grave” sung by a traditional choir based in Kyiv. “Upon arriving to Ukraine, I was surprised to see how much normal life carried on, despite the war,” Haney said. “While the scenes we see in Western media (bombed out villages, injured soldiers, etc) are true and must be seen by the world, I couldn’t help but think that mainstream media is missing half of the story.” “While the front lines footage is harrowing and necessary to show, the things, places, and people worth fighting for, and their everyday stories in extraordinary circumstances, are generally omitted from Western news,” he continued. Emphasizing the universality of their experiences, he said young people, who’ve already gone through the pandemic, are now forced to join the front lines to protect their own. “I’ve met an electronic DJ who enlisted in the army and still performs back home when he is on leave. A nature photographer turned war journalist. Teenagers who now already have 2.5 years of combat experience at the zero line. Lovers pulled apart to different battlegrounds. And as I looked into these faces, I couldn’t help but see parts of myself,” he said. Haney said he recognized himself in many of the young Ukrainians he met, who shared the same dreams, musical tastes and youthful impulses as people elsewhere their age, even as they faced both the realities of war and its psychological toll. He said he hoped the film would bring a more human dimension to the conflict and remind audiences how much people across the world have in common. Charades’ co-founders Carole Baraton and Pierre Mazars said, “Black Sunflowers shows us with stunning subtlety a reality that we, as Europeans, tend to forget: the portrait of a generation of young people whose lives are being shaped — and sacrificed — by the war in Ukraine.” “We are proud to support the film and to see the resonance it is already generating across the international art scene,” added the pair. A music photographer and filmmaker, Haney is best known for the 2014 documentary “No Cameras Allowed,” which grew out of his experiences sneaking into major music festivals including Coachella and filming artists backstage.
