title: ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:00am PT ‘& Juliet’ to Close on Broadway After Four Years By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Ellen Burstyn Wipes Away Tears, Hugs Taika Waititi and Pamela Anderson as Heartfelt Drama ‘Place to Be’ Earns 6-Minute Venice Ovation 20 hours ago Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Aims to Dethrone ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ With $40 Million Debut 23 hours ago Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ 1 day ago See All Matthew Murphy “& Juliet,” a revisionist jukebox musical about Shakespeare’s star-crossed lovers, is closing after four years on Broadway . The upbeat take on “Romeo & Juliet,” which uses Swedish music producer Max Martin’s chart-topping hits to imagine what would happen if Juliet didn’t stab herself with Romeo’s dagger and join in him death, has set its final performance for Jan. 3, 2027. By then, the show will have played 1,723 regular performances and 20 preview performances, putting it among the 50 longest-running Broadway musicals of all time. Luke Sheppard, who is returning to the Great White Way with “Paddington,” directed “& Juliet” while “Schitt’s Creek” alum David West Read wrote the musical’s book. Related Stories Nathan Lane to Be Honored Following 'The Birdcage' 30th Anniversary Screening at Virginia Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) Studio TF1 Smashes Doc Records With ‘Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold,’ Rolls Out ‘Surface’ “& Juliet” opened on Broadway in 2022 after an unsuccessful stint on London’s West End, where the musical’s run was cut short by COVID and had to close without turning a profit. In New York, “& Juliet” broke multiple box office records at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre and became one of the rare post-pandemic musicals to recoup its investment. And the show has translated beyond Broadway with productions in 34 states and nine countries including Germany, Canada and Singapore. The tour has also become profitable, recouping in 2025. Popular on Variety Although “& Juliet” didn’t win any Tony Awards, the musical remained a hot ticket through fun casting choices like TikTok star Charli D’Amelio, ‘N Sync’s Joey Fatone, “Real Housewives” alum Kandi Burruss and Chrissy Metz, as well as special guests like Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. Fatone’s involvement was particularly fitting because “& Juliet” features ‘N Sync songs like “It’s Gonna Be Me.” Martin’s pop anthems, such as, Kelly Clarkson’s “Since U Been Gone,” Britney Spears’ “I’m Not a Girl, Not Yet a Woman” and “Overprotected,” Katy Perry’s “Roar” and Demi Lovato’s “Confident” also help to score Juliet’s new lease on life and love. “& Juliet” ends on a celebratory note, and producers estimate that 8,447 pounds (more than four tons) of confetti have been sprinkled into the audience of the Stephen Sondheim Theatre. “From the very beginning, ‘& Juliet’ has been winning over audiences and critics alike, shattering every stereotype about jukebox musicals to deliver a smart, funny, heartfelt story — all while sparking true joy in everyone who sees it,” producers Theresa Steele Page and Eva Price said. “We’re incredibly proud of the run we’ve had on Broadway, and the story of inclusion, acceptance and second chances we’ve been able to share with more than 1.5 million people in our four years on Broadway.” Louis Messina, Taylor Swift’s Tour Promoter, Urges Judge to Reject Live Nation/Ticketmaster Antitrust Settlement: ‘I Could Go Out of Business Like Other Promoters Who Have Fallen Victim to Live Nation’ Roxette Cancels 40th Anniversary Tour of North American Amphitheaters, Citing ‘Hugely Increased Touring Costs’ Live Nation Posts Continued Growth in Second Quarter With $7.7 Billion in Revenue Loading comments... title: Jack Quaid Jokes He’s a Supermodel After Starring in New Bonobos Campaign: ‘I Guess I Can Add That to My Resume’
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 6:00am PT Jack Quaid Jokes He’s a Supermodel After Starring in New Bonobos Campaign: ‘I Guess I Can Add That to My Resume’ The 'Boys' star says he’s 'come a long way' since his love of wearing 'Family Guy' T-shirts in high school By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest ‘La Bola Negra’ to Open New York City LGBTQ+ Film Festival NewFest (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago Nathan Lane to Be Honored Following ‘The Birdcage’ 30th Anniversary Screening at Virginia Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago ‘The Pitt’ to Be Honored by Cedars-Sinai (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Bonobos If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Jack Quaid isn’t giving up his acting career, but the “Boys” star jokes he’s on his way to becoming a supermodel now that he stars in the Fall 2026 campaign for menswear brand Bonobos. “I guess I can add that to the résumé,” he cracks. The campaign is an episodic video series featuring Quaid in an office setting, where he manages to keep himself — and the Bonobos clothing he’s wearing — together even when thrown some curveballs. Related Stories Arte France’s ‘Tax Me (If You Can)’ Sells to Multiple Territories: ‘Getting Rich People to Talk About Money Was Tough,’ Says Director (EXCLUSIVE) Stefano Knuchel Premieres Final Chapter in 20-Year Hugo Pratt Trilogy With ‘Hugo in Venice’ “I’ve been a fan of the brand for a while now,” Quaid tells me. “I remember wearing a lot of their stuff in the earlier days when they had a brick-and-mortar store near me in L.A. Sometimes as an actor brands reach out and you’re like ‘Yeah, I can sort of see myself partnering with them,’ but with Bonobos, it just felt like the perfect fit. It’s clothes I actually wear.” Popular on Variety In the first episode, Quaid talks to camera and introduces himself as the “Weekday Warrior Consultant.” “That’s not my actual job title. HR keeps rejecting it but that’s what people call me around here because I wear these — the Weekday Warriors,” he says as the camera pans to his pants. “Great-fitting, no-worries work pant. No wrinkles, no hassles.” He goes on to brag that he got others in the office to wear the $119 pants. “But out there,” he says, looking out a window, “there are guys walking around in bad-fitting wrinkly pants that were a ‘great deal’ online — not on my watch.” Future episodes will center on the Weekday Warrior Dress Shirt, Jetsetter Dress Shirt, Everyday Oxford Shirt, Unconstructed Blazer and Knit Blazer. Real Bonobos employees are also featured in the campaign. Quaid admits he wasn’t always one to think about fashion too much. “I’ve come a long way,” he says. “Starting out in like high school, middle school, everything was like a graphic tee with a ‘Family Guy’ quote on it. Nothing against ‘Family Guy,’ but when all of your shirts have a ‘Family Guy’ quote on it, it’s time to maybe have something more basic.” But now, Quaid says, “I consider myself pretty fashionable. I still hang out with a lot of the people I went to high school with, and they’re like, ‘Hey, you dress a lot better than you used to. title: K-Drama Day Returns For Fourth Time On Rakuten Viki With Park Ji Hoon, Bae In Hyuk & More Involved
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Royal Period Drama ‘Queen Silvia’ To Get World Premiere Screening At MIPCOM Cannes Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull Kayleigh Llewellyn Adapting Sarah Waters Novel ‘The Paying Guests’ For BBC Studios Fiction View All September 10, 2026 6:00am Rakuten Viki's K-Drama Day Rakuten Viki EXCLUSIVE: Rakuten Viki ‘s annual K-Drama Day is coming back for a fourth time. title: ‘& Juliet’ To Close In January After Four Years On Broadway
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wicked’ & ‘Wicked: For Good’ Live-To-Film Concerts To Kick Off 2027 Tour In San Francisco & New York ‘Disclosure Day’ Release Date Set At Peacock Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Resigns, Warns AI Industry Is “Gambling With Our Lives” View All September 10, 2026 6:00am '& Juliet' on Broadway Matthew Murphy & Juliet , the Broadway dance-pop jukebox musical that imagines Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet if Juliet hadn’t ended it all after Romeo, will play its final performance on Sunday, January 3, 2027, more than four years after it opened at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre. At its closing, the musical will have played 1,723 regular performances and 20 preview performances, making it one of the 50 longest-running Broadway musicals of all time. Nominated for nine Tony Awards including Best Musical, & Juliet was created by David West Read and features a playlist of hit songs from writer-producer Max Martin including “Since U Been Gone,” “Roar,” “I Want It That Way,” “Confident,” and more. The production is directed by Luke Sheppard with choreography by Jennifer Weber. Related Stories News 'Harry Potter And The Cursed Child' Posts Big Gain As Summer Slips Away - Broadway Box Office News Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd & Sarah Paulson Set Broadway Return In Bess Wohl's 'Small Mouth Sounds' From Producers Scott Rudin & Barry Diller After opening on Broadway on November 17, 2022, & Juliet broke multiple box office records at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre, recouping its $17 million capitalization in 2024, the first new musical of its season to do so. Producers say the production has grossed more than $175 million. Watch on Deadline Last week, & Juliet took in $779,070, a decent amount if not a match for the $1 million-plus grosses of its peak years. Attendance was at about 90% of the Sondheim’s capacity. The Broadway production’s long success though has spurred tours that have played in 73 US cities, nine countries and four continents, producers said. The show currently stars Gianna Harris as ‘Juliet,’ Paulo Szot and Joey Fatone as ‘Lance,’ Alison Luff as ‘Anne,’ Corey Mach as ‘Shakespeare,’ Michael Iván Carrier as ‘May,’ Chrissy Metz as ‘Angélique,’ Ben Jackson Walker as ‘Romeo,’ and Makai Hernandez as ‘François.’ “From the very beginning, & Juliet has been winning over audiences and critics alike, shattering every stereotype about jukebox musicals to deliver a smart, funny, heartfelt story – all while sparking true joy in everyone who sees it,” producers Theresa Steele Page and Eva Price said. “We’re incredibly proud of the run we’ve had on Broadway, and the story of inclusion, acceptance and second chances we’ve been able to share with more than 1.5 million people in our four years on Broadway.” & Juliet is produced on Broadway by Max Martin, Tim Headington, Theresa Steele Page, Jenny Petersson, Martin Dodd and Eva Price. title: Adrienne Warren To Star In ‘Imitation Of Life’ Off Broadway Musical With John Legend Score
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wicked’ & ‘Wicked: For Good’ Live-To-Film Concerts To Kick Off 2027 Tour In San Francisco & New York ‘Disclosure Day’ Release Date Set At Peacock Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Resigns, Warns AI Industry Is “Gambling With Our Lives” View All September 10, 2026 6:00am Adrienne Warren Production Adrienne Warren is set to star in the previously announced Off Broadway musical adaptation of Imitation of Life , the Fannie Hurst novel that spawned two classic Hollywood films. Warren will play Delilah, the role played by Louise Beavers in the 1934 film and by Juanita Moore in Douglas Sirk’s 1959 remake (the character was called Annie in that version). The musical features a book by two-time Pulitzer Prize winner Lynn Nottage, an original score by EGOT winner John Legend and direction by double Tony nominee Whitney White (taking over for the previously announced Liesl Tommy, who remains a producer). Related Stories News Alex Winter Bringing Arthur Miller's 'Incident At Vichy' Revival To Off Broadway Next Year News Sophia Anne Caruso To Star In Duncan Sheik's 'Memoirs Of Amorous Gentlemen' Stage Musical Adaptation The world premiere, six-week limited engagement through January 3, 2027, is set to begin previews on Saturday, November 21, at The Griffin Theater at The Shed. Opening night is Thursday, December 3. Watch on Deadline “It is truly an honor to join this incredible team in bringing Imitation of Life to the stage,” Warren, a Tony winner for her starring role in Broadway’s Tina: The Tina Turner Musical , said in a statement. “Over the years, developing the role of Delilah has become a highlight of my career. She is a character I have grown to love deeply, and I cannot wait to share her with audiences.” Said Legend, “ Imitation of Life tells a deeply emotional story of a remarkable woman’s journey, and I’m thrilled to know that Adrienne Warren will bring Delilah to life. Adrienne is an incredibly gifted performer who brings heart, humanity and radiance to every character she plays. I’m so excited that the world will hear her magnificent voice on the first musical that I’ve composed.” First published in 1933, Hurst’s novel, set in the 1920s and ’30s, tells the stories of two single mothers -one Black, one white – and their daughters as all four build a life together. A central conflict in the story arises when housekeeper Delilah’s daughter attempts to “pass” as white, with the musical addressing such issues as race, identity, motherhood, ambition and belonging. Additional casting, as well as design and creative team members will be announced at a later date. A co-production of The Shed and National Black Theatre, the new musical is produced by National Black Theatre, Universal Theatrical Group, Sue Wagner, John Johnson, Get Lifted Film Co., Crocodile Eyes, LD Entertainment and The Shed. title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Musical Parody Recoups Off Broadway Investment, Extends Run
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wicked’ & ‘Wicked: For Good’ Live-To-Film Concerts To Kick Off 2027 Tour In San Francisco & New York ‘Disclosure Day’ Release Date Set At Peacock Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Resigns, Warns AI Industry Is “Gambling With Our Lives” View All September 10, 2026 6:00am Jay Armstrong Johnson and Jimin Moon in 'Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody' Courtesy Production Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody , Dylan MarcAurele’s buzzy Off Broadway show that began performances at the smallish The Culture Club venue last May, has recouped its initial half-million-dollar investment in its first 13 weeks, producers announced today, adding that the engagement will be extended for a third time. Originally scheduled for an eight-week run at the 174-seat venue – which, prior to this show had been dark for more than a year – the musical is now set to play through Sunday, January 17, 2027. (A previous extension had put the closing date in November.) Related Stories News Alex Winter Bringing Arthur Miller's 'Incident At Vichy' Revival To Off Broadway Next Year News Sophia Anne Caruso To Star In Duncan Sheik's 'Memoirs Of Amorous Gentlemen' Stage Musical Adaptation Producer Alan Kliffer announced the recoupment and latest extension today. Watch on Deadline In a statement, Kliffer and General Manager Christian Palomares said, “This is an extraordinary moment in today’s theatre landscape, especially so for a musical parody about gay hockey players from Canada. Focusing on strong word-of-mouth and moving with deliberate speed in all steps allowed us to grow the show from a fan phenomenon into a musical with its own credibility, and everything since has built on those initial strategies. “This happy moment for our team,” they continued, “is another strong proof point for investing in Off Broadway and redefining what musical parodies can do.” The musical, inspired by the hit TV show that streams on HBO Max, began previews at The Culture Club on Tuesday, May 12, opening on May 26. Prior to The Culture Club engagement, the show was unveiled in eight concert presentations in February and March at the Laurie Beechman Theater and The Bell House. The parody’s approach to the original material is nicely captured in the official synopsis: “ Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody follows starry-eyed golden boy Shane Hollander on his journey from power center to power bottom. Relive all of the moments from the show that made you wet (with tears) up close on the small-stage by an incredible cast of Broadway actors who thought they were auditioning to be in Season 2. Sporting a bop-infused score, scene-stealing cameos by characters like ‘Rose Landry’ and ‘Ilya’s Ass,’ and time jumps absolutely no one can keep track of, audiences will find themselves hot, bothered, and probably saying, ‘….Girl!'” The current cast features Jay Armstrong Johnson as ‘Ilya Rozanov’ and Troy Iwata as ‘Shane Hollander’ (Jimin Moon originated that role), with Ryann Redmond, Cherry Torres and Ryan Duncan rounding out the ensemble. As previously announced, current company member Shelby Acosta will assume the role of ‘Shane’s Mom & Others’ from Torres beginning Thursday, September 10. The creative team for Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody includes MarcAurele (Book, Music, Lyrics and Orchestrations), Alan Kliffer (Direction), Brooke & Tiffany Engen (Choreography), Mateo Chavez Lewis (Music Direction), Sully Ross (Scenic Design), Brendan McCann (Costume Design), Devin Cameron (Lighting Design), Germán Martinez (Sound Design), and Ann James (Intimacy Coordinator/Sensitivity Specialist). An original cast album will be released by Center Stage Records on September 18. Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody is produced by Klif Entertainment and Executive Producer Christian Palomares. title: Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:48am PT Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) Rising Indigenous talents Amber Midthunder, Alyssa Wapanatâhk, and Isabel DeRoy-Olson star as sisters on disparate paths in 1970s L.A. in Marie Clements’ Toronto premiere 'How We Stand' By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago ‘Wolf of the North’ Snares Verve Ventures for North America Ahead of Toronto Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Frontières at TIFF The Market Unveils Lineup, Featuring a ‘Dim Sum Western,’ Newlywed Night of Terror and Wolf-Tracking Dark Comedy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 weeks ago See All Amber Midthunder as Jessie in 'How We Stand,' courtesy of Tombs Production Inc. Writer-director Marie Clements, who premiered “Bones of Crows” in 2022, returns this weekend to the Toronto Film Festival for the world premiere of her latest feature, “How We Stand,” as her new three-part documentary series, “Reclaim My Skin,” waits in the wings for its premiere next month at the Vancouver International Film Festival. Both projects reveal stories of Indigenous women and the power of their actions and voices to bring about necessary change in the world, their communities, and their own lives. Related Stories Remembering the 2006 Emmys, When the Clock Ran Out for Network TV Emmy Overachiever Jason Bateman on Whether He Considers Himself an Actor or Director First “There’s a moment when you’re in the room with matriarchs when everything stands still,” Clement recently told Variety , talking about the doc series for the first time. Popular on Variety “I had the honor to interview Gloria Steinem with Indigenous activists Louise Wakerakats:se Herne and Michelle Schenandoah together in New York last year—even at their most passionate they never spoke over each other,” she said. “They gave space and listened, acknowledging differences while also understanding that we have more in common than what works to divide us.” “Reclaim My Skin” is produced by Marie Clements Media, Screen Siren Pictures and Rezolution Pictures. The series was commissioned by British Columbia’s Knowledge Network in 2024. “How We Stand,” which Clements adapted from her 2011 stage play “Tombs of the Vanishing Indian,” reflects both harsh truths and positive currents of the eras in which it is set. It’s produced by Marie Clements Media and Screen Siren Pictures. Myriad Pictures is handling international sales. Photon Films is the Canadian distributor. Three young Oklahoma sisters and their single mother (Cara Jade Myers, “Killer of the Flower Moon”) travel to L.A. in a 1950s relocation program for Native Americans that promises jobs in big cities. But they were sold a bill of goods. After finding community in the city’s cemented riverways, a tragedy separates the sisters, whose lives take different paths on the shifting cultural landscape of 1970s L.A. “There’s a vibrancy to being alive at any time,” Clements said. “These are modern Indigenous young women who want to grab their futures. They are looking at the world and having a point of view that may or may not land, but are learning who they want to become.” That vibrancy is enhanced by casting of stellar screen stars in the roles of the adult sisters. Amber Midthunder (“Prey,” “Novocaine”) is a doctor who starts a new job at her white husband’s clinic, Alyssa Wapanatâh (“Peter Pan & Wendy”) plays an outspoken activist who starts auditioning for Native American roles in Hollywood movies, while Isabel DeRoy-Olson (AMC’s “Dark Winds”) has the role of a young women adrift and in distress after a traumatic experience she’s trying to figure out. “It was incredible to watch these actors lean in and embody these characters,” Clement says. The stage play was originally commissioned by the Native Voices series at the Autry National Center in L.A. Clements spent time looking through the Autry’s collections in its museums. A colleague’s aunt, who had lived 30 years in the city, told her about the so-called tombs of the riverways where Indigenous people used to meet. “It started me thinking about the underground – where we can go to be together? – as well as the underground policies that were happening at this time,” she continues. The screen adaptation allowed Clement to more deeply explore the worlds suggested in her play. “Starting in Oklahoma with the Technicolor beauty of childhood and this young family and the feeling of possibility – what might happen to a family when they’re given a chance? “But I was also interested in the systems that were happening at the time,” she continues. “We don’t always know that that our lives are being designed by something that we don’t have control of.” While her new film is set in the past, present and future realities ran through the creation and production of “How We Stand.” “I want things to change, I think we all want things to change,” Clement says. “And I found myself thinking about children who are being taken away from their families right now, because our families understand being separated and what that does to the core of a family for generations. “Whether it’s residential school or immigration policies, it’s a profound act to take a member of someone’s family, especially children, away from mothers and fathers. And we’re witnessing that in our time right now. “The fight in the ’70s was around women’s bodies and women’s rights. And that’s trying to be reversed as we speak, so it really does kind of hit you. “Things can feel downtrodden but, you know, there are cool women out there who are still working for change, and that is not going to change.” “How We Stand” has its world premiere at the Toronto International Festival on Sept. 13. title: Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture
full_text: Sep 10, 2026 5:45am PT Toronto’s Indigenous Film and Industry Slates Aim to Grow Audiences and Spark Biz by Reflecting the Diversity of Global Screen Culture 'Predator' series alumni Amber Midthunder and Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi and 'North of North' stars Anna Lambe and Zorga Qaunaq lead the celeb cohort lighting up Toronto's Indigenous screens By Jennie Punter Plus Icon Jennie Punter Latest Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: ‘We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 28 minutes ago ‘Wolf of the North’ Snares Verve Ventures for North America Ahead of Toronto Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Frontières at TIFF The Market Unveils Lineup, Featuring a ‘Dim Sum Western,’ Newlywed Night of Terror and Wolf-Tracking Dark Comedy (EXCLUSIVE) 4 weeks ago See All Zorga Qaunaq as Sesi and Anna Lambe as Yura in 'In the Heart of the South,' courtesy Mixtape VR Inc. and Sphere Media Toronto With enticing acquisition titles, rising talent and supercharged industry presence at the market, the Toronto Intl. Film Festival’s 2026 Indigenous lineup delivers the creative and collaborative screen projects that are increasingly attracting global partners, buyers and audiences. “We’re seeing contemporary Indigenous cinema telling stories within broad historical or present-day contexts but without centering those aspects,” international programmer of U.K., Ireland, Australia and New Zealand and global Indigenous cinema Jason Ryle tells Variety . Related Stories How Did the Emmys’ Documentary Category Get So Star-Studded? 'Widow's Bay,' 'DTF: St. Louis' and 'Spider-Noir' — Despite Its Cancellation — Dominate Creative Arts Emmys Night 2 Winners (FULL LIST) For “How We Stand,” Marie Clements adapts her stage play about separated sisters — played by Amber Midthunder (“Prey”), Alyssa Wapanatâhk (“Little House on the Prairie”) and Isabel DeRoy-Olson (“Dark Winds”) — navigating 1970s political and cultural changes in L.A. Popular on Variety “These are modern Indigenous young women trying to figure their way, just as we all do,” Clements says. “We learn who we are, and who we want to become, through living.” Nyla Innuksuk’s “In the Heart of the South,” one of three Indigenous titles in TIFF section Platform, is a sharp turn from her sci-fi horror “Slash/Back.” Set in the uptight art world, the films stars “North of North” series lead Anna Lambe as an Inuk filmmaker and Zorga Qaunaq (also “North of North”) as the estranged friend who arrives uninvited and rattles her plans. “It’s a sophisticated thriller that critiques arts institutions in Canada from the perspective of an Indigenous person,” says international programmer of Canadian features Kelly Boutsalis. “Brace Your Heart,” Amanda Kernell ’s Sápmi-set Platform feature, follows a young woman who inherits her late father’s reindeer herd and is pressured to accept a local leader’s courtship. “Most of the actors, including the leads, are reindeer herders,” says Ryle. “Amanda has a gift for drawing out performances from people with the smallest suggestions.” Theja Rio’s “Angh” (Platform) centers on a Naga family in a Indo-Burma border village and what happens after the arrival of a Christian missionary. “As far as we can tell, this is the first feature from the Naga people, who are building their own screen culture, as is happening elsewhere in the world, with different means,” Ryle says. The film‘s DP is Adam Pietkiewicz, the recipient of the Variety Artisan Award at TIFF. In his social satire “God Bless You, Mr. Kopu,” Alex Liu casts Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi (“Predator: Badlands”) as a Tongan man drifting from his family while working for an American traveling salesman. The cultures of queer sex workers, hockey players and hip-hop artists are expressed, respectively, in Justin Ducharme’ s chamber drama “Seventeen,” actor-director Cody Lightning’s underdog dramedy “Smudge the Blades” and Alexandra Lazarowich’s doc feature debut “Turtle Island Rap.” “My film explores why it’s hard to be a rapper or beat-maker, and why people still choose to become one,” Lazarowich tells Variety . “The artists are a snapshot of what’s happening in youth culture. The nuances of their Indigenous identity are reflected in the people listening to their music.” Leo Matthew Temela in “In Alaska,” courtesy of IJswater Films, Experimental Forest Films, Uuktumiaq Studios Inspired by a true story, “In Alaska” follows Woody (newcomer Leo Matthew Temela), a depressed teen who is pursued as an eco-terrorist by an FBI agent (Noomi Rapace) after accidentally shooting a hole in an oil pipeline. During an early stage, filmmaker Jaap van Heusden met Inuit actor-director Vinnie Karetak for script notes. They became co-writers and co-directors. “We had to be fearless to keep the heavy subject of suicide in the film and make sure it was never glorified,” Karetak says. “There is a deep sense of loss already from the previous generation that is handed down to human. “When it came to Inuit characters, we collaborated. We talked about every scene, every character, every extra.” Karetak, who acted in “North of North,” says people in the community where the show was flmed helped out on “In Alaska.” “We cast Vinnie’s dog, his son and one of his close friends,” van Heusden recalls. “And we used my ex’s snowmobile,” Karetak adds. The first-ever Filipino-Australian co-production, First Light is the first Tagalog-language film ever submitted by Australia for the Oscars . The drama follows an elderly nun (played by Brilliante Mendoza regular Ruby Ruiz), whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, who, after a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption. Maricel Soriano, Rez Cortez and Kidlat Tahimik co-star. Related Stories TV 'RuPaul's Drag Race UK' Dropped by BBC Movies Mercedes Ron Discusses Prime Video's New YA Romantic Thriller 'Drawn Together' and What's Next for Her Explaining their decision, the Australian Oscar selection committee called First Light “a meditative work about an aging woman who questions her faith as her world begins to crumble around her, leaving an indelible mark.” Robinson’s feature, they said, was “an impressive debut that is a shining example of Australian filmmaking.” First Light was produced by Gabrielle Pearson of Majella Productions and Christelle Lou Dychangco and Jane Pe Aguirre of Clou Media Productions. The film was released in cinemas in the Philippines by Clou Media Productions, and in Australian cinemas by Bonsai Films. Independent Entertainment are handling international sales. First Light has been critically-well received, but, lacking a platform at one of the top-tier A-list fests, the film has been largely overlooked in the awards conversation so far. First Light is Australia’s eighteenth submission in the Best International Feature Film category. Only one Australian film, Bentley Dean and Martin Butler’s Tanna (2015) has ever been nominated for the Best International Feature Oscar. To date, no Australian film has ever won. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will announce the 15 films on the best international feature film shortlist on Dec. 15. The five nominees will be announced Jan. 21, 2027. National Geographic series Africa Earth’s Wild Home has captured the elusive amphibians — and other species — on camera for television for the first time ever. title: ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Game Director Naoki Hamaguchi On Taking Risks With Beloved Characters: “One Wrong Decision” Could Get Him “Shouted At”; Teases TV Show Potential
full_text: Skip to main content By Destiny Jackson Destiny Jackson Crafts Editor, Awards @DestinyDreadful More Stories By Destiny ‘Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival’ Video Game Devs On Making The Franchise “Nobly Provocative” In The Modern Age ‘Saw: Genesis’ Creative Director Talks Multiplayer Build, Expanding The ‘Saw’ Mythology & Putting Players Through The Wringer Emmys Night 2 Craft Awards Predict Smooth Sailing For ‘Widow’s Bay’ Alongside Celebrating ‘The Pitt’ & ‘DTF St. Louis’ View All September 10, 2026 5:00am Final Fantasy VII Revelation Square Enix Looks like those seven seconds are coming to an end. At Gamescom 2026, Final Fantasy VII Revelation offered a glimpse at the enormous final chapter of Square Enix ’s remake trilogy, which concludes Cloud and his activist friends’ journey as they race against time to stop Sephiroth, who is close to attaining god status in his quest to harm the planet. The preview dropped us into Chapter 4 aboard Cid’s iconic Highwind aerial ship with Yuffie, Barret, Cait Sith and Vincent, as the group explores the islands for resources or makes a beeline for Wutai, which has been significantly expanded for the finale. Meanwhile, Tifa and an unwell Cloud remain separated from the group, leaving the rest of the party to chart their own course through a world that has grown considerably since Rebirth . Related Stories News Mory Sacko Prepares 'Food Samurai' For Disney+ North America News 'Kane Chronicles' Live-Action Series In Development At Disney+ For Square Enix game director Naoki Hamaguchi , who has guided the project through Final Fantasy VII Remake and Rebirth , that expansion is one of the biggest challenges—and opportunities—of the finale. The Highwind opens the skies, while flying chocobos and parachuting offer new ways to traverse familiar territory. Junon bears the brunt of Weapons’ attacks in defense of the planet, parts of Gongaga have been flooded, and the grasslands look remarkably different from above. Watch on Deadline After Remake ’s more linear structure and Rebirth ’s open-world expansion, Revelation takes that scale to a planet-wide level. Hamaguchi said the Highwind provides “a feeling that no other open-world game gives,” while Mai and the game’s side content help guide players through the sprawling landscape without making exploration too stressful. During the timed playthrough (and despite all the exploratory distractions), I caught a hopeful glimpse of a finale geared towards delving deeper into the lore of its iconic cast of characters. Hamaguchi told Deadline that the team painstakingly cemented Vincent and Yuffie into irrevocable mainstays while also giving Zack (not available in my preview) an increasingly important role in the trilogy’s larger time-boggling mystery. Below, Deadline spoke further with Hamaguchi about bringing the ambitious remake project to its conclusion, expanding its world and characters, Cloud’s emotional journey, and whether Final Fantasy VII could eventually leap to television. DEADLINE: This is it. You’re in the process of finalizing one of the biggest remake projects of a legendary game for Square Enix. What is the general vibe and emotionality going through your minds right now at headquarters? NAOKI HAMAGUCHI: As you say, it is a legendary game. It’s so well-loved by so many people out there, with really high expectations, and I’m remaking that. And in doing the final work, it’s really setting in that we’re about to release the climax. There’s a feeling of great satisfaction, and I’m feeling that now. I can still remember when we put out Final Fantasy VII Rebirth ; the big challenge with that game was that we wanted to take that classic Final Fantasy feel and bring it into an open-world structure. And I think we felt that we did that really well, and thankfully, there was a very positive reaction to that. So, with Revelation , what we’ve tried to do is take that even further and expand out. And it sits on a planet-level open world, with verticality, and the whole environment is now available for adventure. And I’m very confident that we’ve done that. And really, there’s no open world out there at this scale in any other game. Final Fantasy VII Revelation Square Enix DEADLINE: With that said, I know Final Fantasy VII Remake faced backlash for being too linear. Then Rebirth opened up a lot as you’ve stated. And now this one’s even bigger. Are you worried about an unwieldy narrative or fans’ response to this? HAMAGUCHI: Whatever kind of game you’re making, you can have 100 people and show them the game; you’re never going to get anything where all 100 of them like it. There’ll always be someone who doesn’t like it, who complains about it. You can’t reduce those voices to nothing, so we don’t even try. What’s important is that you have a solid concept and do your best to achieve it. With Revelation , I really am confident that we managed to do that. So, again, you guys played the demos and had this experience, but that feeling of just the size of the world and that scale of open world, when you get up in the Highwind and you set out into the skies, I don’t think there’s any other open-world game out there that will give you that feeling. So, I want to share that feeling with as many people as possible and show what we’ve achieved here. DEADLINE: Does this mean we can expect the chicken with the tin can in Gongaga to appear again? HAMAGUCHI: No, I was thinking about what to do with that for a long time. We’ve taken a slightly different approach [laughs]. But we’ve got a lot of quests like that, with that distinctive Final Fantasy humor in it. Look forward to loads of that. Final Fantasy VII Revelation Square Enix DEADLINE: Who was the character you understood more by the end of the game’s journey? HAMAGUCHI: Vincent and Yuffie because they were two characters in the original who were optional characters. And because of that, they weren’t featured within the main story as strongly as all the other cast. So, as a very conscious decision for the Remake series, they’ve been made compulsory parts of the team, and they’ve really been fleshed out more and given the background and the deeper dive into them as characters. So, I think those are probably the two the fans will appreciate most and that have been fleshed out the most. Also, Zack is the other one because he plays a very interesting role in the story’s setup. He gives the impression of, “Well, this is the [game] differences, this is what is going on.” Similarly to Rebirth , in terms of showing not telling, he will also have a role like that in Revelation . So players can very much expect to see a lot more of Zack and dig even deeper into him. He plays a very massive part in this last finale of the series. DEADLINE: Which character then was the most difficult to flesh out and bring to the forefront? HAMAGUCHI: That’s a tough question. In some ways, Zack was quite a difficult one. Because first of all, he’s quite well covered in terms of background material from the compilation. There’s a lot of information about him where he features quite heavily, so there’s stuff we have to include. And at the same time, the way he’s used in the story, he’s part of that very special metaphysical phenomenon that’s going on. So, how he’s portrayed in that, and how he interacts with others and the environment, have to be handled very carefully so that we don’t give too much away. Getting that balance right with Zack was hard, especially in adding more detail about him. But thinking about this question again, and all the characters, they’ve got really dedicated fans. You make one wrong decision for any of them, I’m probably going to get shouted at by a lot of people [laughs]. So, I think picking one as more difficult than the others is quite difficult in itself. DEADLINE: In the preview’s Chapter 4, Cloud is already suffering from mako poisoning. But it was interesting to me that Mai mentions the Lifesprings may be involved in restoring or improving his mental state? What can you tell us about this new development? My boy is suffering. title: Jimmy Kimmel’s Interview With James Talarico Heading to YouTube to Avoid FCC Hassle
full_text: × Skip to main content THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Uniting the biggest names in Hollywood with the athletic stars they admire most close By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All September 10, 2026 2:48am From left: Jimmy Kimmel, James Talarico and Brendan Carr. Kevin Winter/Getty Images; Rick Kern/Getty Images for Vox Media; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Jimmy Kimmel ‘s planned Thursday interview with James Talarico will not be aired on the ABC broadcast of Jimmy Kimmel Live! and will instead stream on the late-night show’s YouTube channel. Kimmel made the announcement during his monologue on Wednesday’s episode of his late-night show. Discussing the Texas Senate race, Kimmel said that he would interview Democratic candidate Talarico on Thursday “under unusual circumstances,” and then alluded to ABC’s ongoing issues with the Federal Communications Commission. “You know, for a lot of years, for the whole 20-plus years of our show, in fact, I’ve been interviewing Americans who are running for office with no problem at all, just like Letterman did, Leno did, Arsenio, etc. etc., I’ve interviewed a lot of political candidates. From Hilary Clinton to Ted Cruz to Donald Trump,” Kimmel said. “I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015, and at that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates. In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016. But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed.” Related Stories TV No Decisions Made on 'Jimmy Kimmel Live!' Future TV Adele Zaikman on Winning 'DWTS: The Next Pro' and Daniella Karagach's Advice for Season 35 “Now that [Trump is] president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates [and] our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings, it would seem, [that] they don’t like,” Kimmel added, referring to ABC’s ongoing battle with the FCC and in particular with the agency’s chair Brendan Carr . In September 2025, in the aftermath of the assassination of Charlie Kirk, Carr condemned Kimmel for comments he made during one of his monologues about Kirk’s death, and the FCC chair intimated that regulatory action or license reviews for ABC affiliates could happen if Kimmel wasn’t made to apologize. After Kimmel was temporarily suspended over the matter, a firestorm engulfed ABC’s owner, Disney. Kimmel became a cause celebre in Hollywood and he was eventually reinstated but that didn’t stop the FCC from continuing to target ABC, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and the daytime talk show The View over claims they didn’t meet the agency’s equal time requirements . In August this year, ABC said it was suing the FCC over the agency’s efforts to challenge its broadcast licenses and the content of The View , saying that it is a free speech violation by the Trump administration. On Wednesday, Kimmel confessed that ABC’s ongoing issues with the FCC meant that the Talarico interview would instead air online. “Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Terico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV. So if you want to learn about a candidate for the Senate tomorrow, you will have to go to the Jimmy Kimmel Live! YouTube channel, where you will see it in its entirety. And thank goodness we have that because in the America we live in right now, that is the best that we can do until November.” The latest brouhaha between Jimmy Kimmel Live! and the FCC comes amid speculation that the late night show may come to an end in 2027. On Tuesday, Page Six reported that the long-running ABC talk show would end next year. A source close to Kimmel denied to The Hollywood Reporter there was any truth to the report. This also isn’t the first time an interview with Talarico has caused such consternation on late-night television. In February, Stephen Colbert, the host of the now-ended Late Show , revealed on air that lawyers for CBS blocked him from interviewing Talarico on broadcast, citing the FCC’s new guidance for political candidates on talk shows. The Late Show ran the Talarico interview on its YouTube channel, where it has been viewed 9.5 million times. THR

title: Kayleigh Llewellyn Adapting Sarah Waters Novel ‘The Paying Guests’ For BBC Studios Fiction
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Royal Period Drama ‘Queen Silvia’ To Get World Premiere Screening At MIPCOM Cannes Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull Kayleigh Llewellyn Adapting Sarah Waters Novel ‘The Paying Guests’ For BBC Studios Fiction View All September 10, 2026 2:56am Kayleigh Llewellyn and Sarah Waters Getty, Charlie Hopkinson EXCLUSIVE: Every book in the canon of British author Sarah Waters has been adapted for screen – except one. That’s about to change. Deadline understands BBC Studios Fiction has optioned The Paying Guests , the 2014 book about a 1922 love affair that turns into a twisting crime thriller. We hear In My Skin and Killing Eve writer Kayleigh Llewellyn , who is penning the upcoming BBC series The Dream Lands , is attached to adapt it as a series. No network or streamer is attached at this stage. Here’s the plotline: “Set in London in 1922, The Paying Guests follows Frances Wray and her mother as they take in married lodgers Lilian and Leonard Barber. What begins as a clandestine, intoxicating love affair between Frances and Lilian spirals into a twisting crime thriller, culminating in a brutal murder and a nail‑biting court case.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News BBC Studios Launches High-End Drama Label Led By 'Good Omens' EP Josh Cole News 'Bridgerton's Queen Charlotte Boards BBC's 'The Dream Lands' Waters, who has been shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize and Women’s Prize For Fiction, is one of the most adapted authors working today. Previous adaptations of her books include BBC series Tipping the Velvet and Fingersmith , Andrew Davies’ Affinity , BBC telemovie The Night Watch and Lenny Abrahamson’s feature The Little Stranger . Fingersmith was also the inspiration for Park Chan‑wook’s The Handmaiden . The Paying Guests will join a BBC Studios Fiction slate that includes the upcoming third season of Jimmy McGovern drama Time , which is set in a Young Offenders Institution and stars David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran. BBC Studios Fiction was created last year, as we revealed at the time, with BBC Studios Comedy boss Josh Cole at the top as Chief Creative Officer. The label sits alongside BBC Studios Drama Productions, which makes long-running, continuing and returning series such as Casualty and Silent Witness . Other labels include Trying maker BBC Studios Comedy, Baby Reindeer producer Clerkenwell, Sherwood maker House, Firebird Pictures ( Wahala ), Lookout Point ( Pride and Prejudice ), Baby Cow ( Changing Ends ) and Killing Eve producer Sid Gentle. title: cut 340 jobs
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Channel 4 To Combine Drama & Comedy Teams Under Historic Jobs Cull Channel 4 To Merge Unscripted Units, Slashing Commissioning Roles In Half ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race UK’ Canceled By BBC Amid “Financial Pressures” View All September 9, 2026 4:00am Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Channel 4/Getty Channel 4 has announced the deepest round of layoffs in its 43-year history. The British network, home to shows including The Great British Bake Off and Taskmaster , is planning to cut 340 jobs by the end of 2026, meaning its workforce will shrink by more than a quarter. Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra announced the layoffs on Wednesday after spending recent months overseeing a strategic review of the commercial broadcaster. Related Stories Culture List Of Hollywood & Media Layoffs From Paramount To Warner Bros Discovery To CNN & More News Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Resigns, Warns AI Industry Is “Gambling With Our Lives” She told employees that the redundancies — equivalent to 28% of Channel 4’s 1,276-strong workforce — will ensure that more of C4’s £1 billion ($1.3 billion) income is spent onscreen. The scale of the cuts has shocked insiders and others close to Channel 4. One source described it as a “very bad” day for the British broadcaster. Watch on Deadline Channel 4 finds itself increasingly isolated in a world in which it is dwarfed in size by some of its production suppliers, rival networks and digital giants like YouTube. The state-owned broadcaster is grappling with these forces at the same time as reckoning with ad market contraction and rising production costs. Dogra has designed a new organizational structure, aimed at reducing management layers, removing duplication and simplifying decision-making. She is positioning the changes as “owning our future,” building on the work of her predecessor Alex Mahon in growing digital sales to 34% of Channel 4’s revenue. Channel 4’s announcement was, however, light on details about the new structure, including how it will impact commissioning and the network’s fledgling in-house production plans. A consultation process with staff will begin shortly. Channel 4 said further details will be announced about the plans in the coming months. Dogra said: “Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK. We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won’t, reach audiences others can’t, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations. “Today marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love. “The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation. Many talented people who have made an enormous contribution to Channel 4 will be leaving as a result. “These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4 that can invest a greater proportion of revenues into distinctive content, back British creativity and deliver impact for audiences long into the future.” Channel 4 chair Geoff Cooper added: “The proposals announced today are intended to secure Channel 4’s future as a trusted, independent British broadcaster. “By taking action now, it can build a more sustainable and resilient organisation, maximise investment in content and strengthen its ability to deliver public value for audiences, the creative industries and the UK for the years ahead.” Caroline Dinenage, chair of UK Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee, said the jobs cull was “deeply worrying” for Channel 4’s employees. “Channel 4 is a unique asset and must find ways to maintain independence and distinctiveness while capitalising on efficiencies and opportunities for collaboration,” she added. Channel 4’s job cuts follow similar redundancies at the BBC, which has committed to reducing its workforce by 10%, equating to around 2,000 layoffs. Channel 4’s last major round of redundancies came in 2024, when 200 roles were closed. Channel 4 cuts often spark conversations about the broadcaster’s executive pay, which reached record levels during Mahon’s tenure. Despite leaving Channel 4 in June 2025, Mahon’s total pay stood at £566,000, which is more than the BBC director-general earns in a year, despite running a considerably larger organization. PRIYA DOGRA EMAIL TO CHANNEL 4 STAFF: Thank you for joining the All Staff meeting today and I know many of you will now be in follow-up meetings with your ExCo member to understand what the announcement means for your role and your area. I appreciate this is a significant and unsettling moment for many of you, but particularly for those whose roles will be affected by the changes we are proposing. I want to be clear that we have not made these proposals lightly. They will affect many talented people who have contributed enormously to our success. Our intention is to support people through the process with care, respect and transparency. A lot of detail was covered in the All Staff, so I want to briefly summarise the key points. What I presented today is the first stage of our transformation strategy. This work is designed to help us prioritise investment in content, grow our impact and secure our long-term sustainability. We have proposed a new organisational design that will significantly decrease non-programming spend by reducing our overall headcount by approximately 340 roles, equivalent to 28% of our workforce, by the end of the year. These proposals are intended to create a simpler, more focused organisation and allow us to direct a greater proportion of our revenues towards distinctive British content. That investment is what allows us to have impact. But this transformation is not just about reducing costs. It is also about creating the platform for future growth, strengthening our revenues so that we can invest more in the content, creativity and public value that set Channel 4 apart well into the future. I explained why these changes are necessary: · The market around us has changed faster than expected. Audiences and advertisers are increasingly moving towards global platforms, while many of our competitors are becoming larger and better funded. Advertiser investment in UK television has fallen by more than £400 million since 2019 and is expected to decline further over the next five years. · At the same time, as a publicly owned, commercially funded broadcaster, we have fewer levers than many other organisations. We cannot simply cut profits to absorb financial pressure. Since 2019, while our revenue has remained broadly stable, our operating costs have increased by 25%. That means operating costs now account for a greater proportion of our revenue. In 2019, running Channel 4 cost us around 32p for every £1 of revenue we generated. Today that figure is around 40p. That means less of our revenue is available to invest in programmes, and as that declines, so does our ability to drive audience and revenue growth. That is not sustainable, and it is not what Channel 4 is here to do. · The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we are organised and how we operate. The proposed changes have been developed through a comprehensive review of roles, structures and ways of working across the organisation. They focus on reducing management layers, simplifying decision-making and removing duplication, so that we can build a leaner, more efficient operating model ready for the future. · Our overall goal is to spend more of our revenue on content, because content is how Channel 4 delivers impact. Our purpose matters more than ever: to tell stories others don’t, provide trusted news, represent the UK in all its diversity and remain a distinctive British public service broadcaster. By making difficult decisions today and reshaping our organisation now, we can create a more sustainable cost base so we can protect and strengthen that impact and secure Channel 4 as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for years to come. Work on our future strategic direction is well advanced and will be shared in the coming months. At its heart, the transformation’s theme is ‘owning our future’: reshaping how we reach audiences through distribution, partnerships and platforms; enabling greater investment in distinctive programmes that set Channel 4 apart; and ensuring resources are allocated to maximise long-term value, sustainability and public impact. Today’s announcement is the first stage of that transformation and is an important step towards delivering those goals. I know that the next few weeks are going to be very difficult, particularly for those directly impacted, but also for those of you whose teammates will be going through the process. We will continue to share updates throughout this process, and I will also be travelling to each of our offices in the coming weeks to meet with you, hear your views and answer questions – details will follow. I want to thank you in advance for the professionalism and care I know you will show to each other, and for everything you will continue to do for Channel 4. In Italy , cinemas enjoyed their best-ever June-August period, with 20.8 million admissions and €162.3 million in box office receipts. That is the strongest August ever recorded in the country. title: ‘No Other Land’ Co-Directors Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor Lift Lid On New Bombshell Doc ‘Naza’ Exposing Israel’s Deliberate Targeting Of Civilian Homes In Gaza – Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Ellen Burstyn Talks Working Into 90s with Starring Role In Unexpected Love Story ‘Place To Be’; Pays Tribute To Gloria Steinem – Venice First Behind-The Scenes Look Reveals Isabelle Huppert As Crime Boss In Yann Demange’s London-Set ‘Lineage’ LevelK Posts U.S. & Euro Sales Haul For Karlovy Vary Prizewinner ‘The Guest’ View All September 10, 2026 4:10am Naza The Guardian/JW Films Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor hit the Venice Film Festival on Thursday with bombshell late competition addition Naza . Based on interviews with 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers, the documentary exposes the AI, phone surveillance and crude points-based systems deployed by the Israeli military in Gaza to decide targets, Hamas-related or otherwise, and then take them out in their homes regardless of whether children and other family members are likely to be killed in the strike as well. The title Naza is taken from the Israeli military’s Hebrew acronym to describe each individual that could die when tallying up an estimated death-toll ahead of a strike. Related Stories News Elon Musk Embarks On Vicious Rant About "Bitter Old Man" Alex Gibney & Threatens To Sue Over 'Musk' Documentary Festivals 'DAU': First Teaser From Ilya Khrzhanovsky's Epic Venice Competition Title The film also contains allegations that Israel is systematically destroying homes in Gaza to create a wasteland that will prevent Palestinians from ever returning, and also deliberately taking out figures from civil society such as journalists and medical staff. Watch on Deadline It follows and builds on Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land , winner of the Best Documentary Academy Award in 2025, co-directed with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting Israeli army-backed efforts to erase the West Bank Palestinian villages of Masafer Yatta, while painting a wider picture of Israeli occupation. “Our film is showing that the basic targeting unit of the Israeli targeting systems is a family home in Gaza,” Abraham told Deadline ahead of the world premiere. “That’s how it operates. Every building in Gaza, every home in Gaza has a number. The system is designed to locate targets. When they are in civilian spaces, when they go back home, that is one of, for me, one of the most striking revelations of the film. A revelation, of course, that I think should have been known to people by the fact that they should have listened to Palestinians in Gaza who are saying it. But to hear it from the inside for me was quite striking.” The world premiere comes amid growing condemnation of Israel’s military campaign in the Palestinian territory – sparked by Hamas’s slaughter of 1,200 people in Southern Israel on October 7, 2023 – which has since killed more than 73,000 people and injured close to 175,000 others, while destroying key infrastructure and 90% of homes. The film is based on investigative reporting carried out by Abraham in the wake of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and the launch of Israel’s retaliatory military campaign on October 27 of that same year, the findings of which were previously published by The Guardian, which is a producer on the film, and Israeli news outlets +972 and Local Call. “I had spent time already before October 7 with +972 magazine and Local Call, and later with The Guardian, investigating the Israeli military, the Israeli targeting systems, Israel’s reliance on AI, on big data and mass surveillance of Palestinians,” he said, explaining how he had managed to connect with the interviewees in the film through a network built across years. Co-director Szor, who is also cinematographer on the film, kept a low media profile during the festival run and awards campaign for No Other Land , but joins Abraham in the interviews for Naza in Venice. “It’s true with No Other Land , I was not vocal, it’s just my personality,” said Szor, when quizzed on how their partnership works. “As directors, we just talk about everything, what exactly are we looking for; the questions that need to be asked… the structure, what story we will tell, and then, cinematically, where will we film the interviews and what else will we show beyond the interviews,” she explained. The anonymous silhouetted testimonies at the heart of the film are framed as rooftop interviews against the nighttime skyline of Tel Aviv, which aside from being one of the most liberal cities in the world is also the beating heart of Israel’s military apparatus and home to its HaKirya HQ. The physical appearances and voices of the interviewees have been altered to hide their identities. “As you can imagine, we went through a very rigorous process with The Guardian’s investigations desk which is an expert in that field… we’ve taken extraordinary measures,” said Abraham of the efforts to protect his sources, adding the aim was also to ensure the interviews did not come over as “robotic” as a result. “That was important for us because we wanted the testimonies to land and to be impactful,” he explains, highlighting that the anonymized interviewees are real people and not actors voicing transcripts. The testimonies are chilling, with multiple interviewees explaining they are part of a system that they are powerless to challenge, evoking unspoken references to Adolf Eichman, who managed the logistics of the Holocaust, and Hannah Arendt’s coverage of his trial in Jerusalem in which she coined the phrase “banality of evil”. “It’s something that came up from some of the soldiers themselves. It’s one of the things that surprised me. Of course, I think about Second World War and the Holocaust, and I think our obligation is to draw universal lessons from that, because when we say never again, how can we say that if we are not drawing the universal lessons, the universal opposition to dehumanization, to turning people into numbers,” said Abraham. “I was surprised how much soldiers themselves sometimes, not all of them, but some of them, spoke about it too. I mean we have a soldier in the film who talks about how after being involved in the killing of so many civilians and seeing their humanity kind of evaporate, he thought about German society in the 30s and the 40s. He felt he could understand something about that, that he couldn’t understand before.” “To me, in a world where so many people use the memory of the Holocaust in a way to justify what is happening in Gaza, and it is important to think about how can we draw from that period of time to oppose dehumanization, to oppose killing, no matter who the person is being killed, and that’s not to say that it’s the same, but it is to say that we are finding these similarities that exist throughout many cases of genocide.” In between the interview segments, the documentary cuts to footage of the aftermath of Israeli strikes in Gaza as family members desperately try to dig out victims from underneath collapsed buildings, as well as shots into Tel Aviv homes as people serenely go about their lives in the evening. Asked if this was meant as a deliberate parallel between the lives of people living in Tel Aviv and those in Gaza, some 40 miles to the south, Abraham says it goes beyond that and is more a comment on Israel’s bombing of civilian homes on the basis of intelligence that a person of interest is present. “Our film shows, it could have been someone selected by AI, it would have been someone who the army decides is somehow related to Hamas, it could have been someone that they targeted for other reasons, the mere fact they are physically present in a building, where there is no military activity, justifies bombing the building and killing everyone inside,” said Abraham. “If you apply these kinds of standards to any place in the world, and especially Tel Aviv, that gives you an endless stream of justifications to bomb pretty much any civilian building, any shopping mall, any cinema… Houses are not bombed because Hamas are firing rockets from them, which is what we’ve consistently heard from intelligence officers. The houses are bombed because it’s easier to bomb people and to find them when they go home to sleep at night.” Asked on how he got military personnel to speak so candidly, Abraham suggests he filled a void, with his quest helped by the lack of coverage of what was going on in Gaza in Israel’s mainstream media. “Mainstream Israeli media is totally uninterested in asking these questions, in asking soldiers about the actions that they’ve done, which have contributed to the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. A polite way to say it, would be to say that they ignored the atrocities in Gaza. But if I’m being honest, it’s not that they ignored it; it’s that they very often created the justification and normalized very genocidal, very scary ideas about the population in Gaza, and I really think they bear some of the responsibility for what happens,” he said. “When you operate as an Israeli journalist in a space where the majority of the mainstream kind of legacy Israeli media are not asking these questions, then you have an advantage because when you start asking these questions, then slowly… you find the answers,” he continued. Abraham says mainstream channels could equally connect with the subjects in his film, and confirm the revelations in Naza, but suggests they will not because in his view they are “complicit in the killing”. Digging into that allegation he suggests that while a handful of Israeli news outlets such as Haaretz and +972 Magazine have been critical of the military campaign in Gaza they are the exception to the rule. “The majority of the society watches the TV channels: Channel 13, Channel 12, Channel 11,” said Abraham, citing Israeli research into local TV coverage of the military campaign in Gaza. “In the first six months of the onslaught in Gaza, this period of time when about 10,000 children are being killed by Israel, Channel 12, the mainstream Israeli channel, dedicated less than 0.5% of its news items and news coverage to talk about the civilian casualties in Gaza… there are journalists far more talented than us in Israel that have been asking these questions, but the majority of the media has ignored, justified, incited, and therefore is partially responsible, I think, for the killing in Gaza.” As the film debuts in Venice both directors hope the exploration of Abraham’s previously published findings will travel wider on the big screen. “There is something different about seeing it on screen and seeing people talking about it from reading it, so hopefully it will have a big impact. It will reach more people. I think we’re also using our privileges because we’ve done No Other Land , and it reached Oscar. That also was for us just a motivation to make another film because we hope that it will reach a big stage,” said Szor. “It’s weird to be in a festival with this kind of film, which is so heavy and on such a hard topic, but it’s very important to show it in the biggest stage there is.” Historic Job Cull Will See Mergers In Unscripted & Scripted Divisions Interview With Oscar Winners About Bombshell New Gaza Doc; Reviews ‘Practical Magic 2’ Looks To Cast Post-Summer Spell With $58M-$63M: Preview ‘Charlie’s Angels’ & ‘Buffy’ Reunions In Play As First Presenters Are Revealed Read More About: Comments

full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wicked’ & ‘Wicked: For Good’ Live-To-Film Concerts To Kick Off 2027 Tour In San Francisco & New York ‘Disclosure Day’ Release Date Set At Peacock Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Resigns, Warns AI Industry Is “Gambling With Our Lives” View All April 30, 2026 7:26am John Legend Alberto Rodriguez/Variety via Getty Images UPDATE, with production dates : Imitation of Life , the new musical with a book by Lynn Nottage , music and lyrics by John Legend , and direction by Liesl Tommy will begin performances on Wednesday, September 9, at The Griffin Theater at The Shed Off Broadway . A co-production of The Shed and National Black Theatre, Imitation of Life will play a strictly limited four- week presentation engagement through Sunday, October 4. In the announcement today, the production was described as The Shed’s “first major step in nurturing and developing a new American musical. The musical will be performed with full cast and live orchestra. Related Stories News Alex Winter Bringing Arthur Miller's 'Incident At Vichy' Revival To Off Broadway Next Year News Sophia Anne Caruso To Star In Duncan Sheik's 'Memoirs Of Amorous Gentlemen' Stage Musical Adaptation Additional details including casting, design and creative team members will be announced at a later date. Watch on Deadline PREVIOUS, February 12: A new stage adaptation of the Fannie Hurst novel Imitation of Life , featuring music and lyrics by Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony Award winner John Legend and a book by Pulitzer Prize winner Lynn Nottage, will premiere at the Off Broadway venue The Shed this coming fall, producers announced today. Liesl Tommy ( Eclipsed ) will direct. The Shed staging at its Griffin Theater is a co-production with National Black Theatre. Additional details for the limited engagement including casting, design and creative teams and production dates will be announced at later. The musical is based on both the 1933 novel and the famed 1934 and 1959 Universal Pictures adaptations. The ’33 film directed by John M. Stahl starred Claudette Colbert, Louise Beavers, Fredi Washington and Rochelle Hudson; Douglas Sirk’s 1959 version starred Lana Turner, Juanita Moore, Sandra Dee and Susan Kohner. The synopsis: “ Imitation of Life follows two single mothers, one Black and one White, as well as their daughters, who build a shared life while each strives for success and love in a society divided by race and class. Set across the vibrant backdrop of 1920s Atlantic City and 1930s New York, this new, profoundly moving musical explores themes of identity, the American Dream, and what we leave for future generations.” In a joint statement, Nottage, Legend and Tommy said today: “Originally published in 1933, novelist Fannie Hurst’s Imitation of Life tells the story of two women, one Black and one white, struggling to raise their daughters in a world shaped by inequalities. While the novel’s narrative is very much a product of its time, its themes of race, class, and gender in America continue to resonate today. As artists, we are drawn to Imitation of Life ’s enduring emotional power and its potential to be reimagined in ways that feel both contemporary and urgent. It has been a profound joy to collaborate on bringing this story to the stage, and we are thrilled to premiere this musical at The Shed, where we look forward to sharing the beautiful and deeply moving journey of Delilah and Peola Johnston with audiences.” The project marks Legend’s first major musical stage endeavor as a composer. He was a producer on both Ain’t Too Proud in 2019 and Jitney in 2017, and contributed the song “(I Guess I) Miss You” to SpongeBob SquarePants in 2017.
